findings.failure_scenario: An ICP facet requests corpus_config { collections: ['aristotle_primary'], min_relevance: 0.75, max_chunks: 40 }. hybridSearch ignores all of it, runs `this.semanticSearch(semanticQuery, { maxChunks: 20, minRelevance: 0.6 })` (:353-356) and `this.keywordSearch(keywords, { maxChunks: 20 })` (:357), then returns `merged.slice(0, this.DEFAULT_MAX_CHUNKS)` — 10 chunks (:369, :47). The facet asked for 40 scoped chunks and got 10 unscoped ones.
findings.consequence: The entire per-facet retrieval configuration surface of the ICP pipeline is inert. Worse, in the per-collection branch (:149-182) the N parallel calls are *byte-identical* at the cache-key level (buildCacheKey at :337-341 hashes only prefix+query+keywords+weights), so N collections produce N identical result sets that then collapse to one under the `docId:page_start` dedupe at :176.
findings.fix_sketch: Add a fourth `options?: Partial<RetrievalOptions>` parameter to hybridSearch, thread it into the two internal searches and into buildCacheKey, and honour maxChunks instead of DEFAULT_MAX_CHUNKS. ~15 lines. Separately: make `npm run typecheck` a pre-commit gate, otherwise this class of defect recurs.

findings.claim: A transient ChromaDB failure at first use permanently disables retrieval for the whole process AND poisons the cache with empty results for 30 minutes — while retrieveContext's own comment claims it throws on infrastructure errors.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:138-140 — `this.logger.warn(...); this.collectionResolved = true; return;` (no UUID configured, still marked resolved).
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:153-155 and :173-175 — same pattern; `collectionResolved` is set true on every failure path and there is no reset anywhere in the file.
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:920 — the query URL is built from `${this.COLLECTION_ID}`, which stays `''` (set at :111).
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:947-953 — `if (!chromaResponse.ok) { ... this.logger.error(...); return []; }` — swallowed, not thrown.
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:303 — `this.setCache(cacheKey, expanded);` runs unconditionally, including when `expanded` is `[]`.
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:209-212 — `const cached = this.getFromCache(cacheKey); if (cached) { return cached; }` — `[]` is truthy in JS, so a cached empty result short-circuits every retry.
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:306-313 — the catch says "F-13: Throw on infrastructure errors instead of silently returning []" and the orchestrator's "circuit breaker handles the case where ALL queries fail".
findings.failure_scenario: ChromaDB is still starting when the daemon boots. resolveCollectionId's fetch throws, no collectionId is configured, so COLLECTION_ID stays '' and collectionResolved is latched true. Every subsequent query POSTs to `.../collections//query`, gets a 404, semanticSearch returns [], retrieveContext caches [] for that key and returns it. The comment's circuit breaker never fires because semanticSearch never lets an error reach the catch at :306.
findings.consequence: A drafting run against a briefly-unavailable Chroma produces a document with zero corpus grounding, reported as a successful run, with cached empty results guaranteeing the next 30 minutes of runs are equally empty. The stated F-13 fail-loud guarantee is defeated one call frame below where it is documented.
findings.fix_sketch: (1) Do not cache empty result arrays (`if (expanded.length > 0) this.setCache(...)`). (2) Only latch `collectionResolved` on success; on failure leave it false so the next call retries. (3) Throw from semanticSearch on non-ok HTTP so the documented catch at :306 actually receives it. ~12 lines.

findings.claim: The +0.10 canonical-term boost is additive on top of the cross-encoder score and clamped to 1.0, so it saturates the top of the distribution and lets low-ranked chunks jump above the reranker's best hits. The project's own evaluation concluded the reranker is the win; this step overwrites it.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:239-241 — `const reranked = opts.rerank ? await this.rerankResults(query, diverse) : diverse;`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1262 — `relevanceScore: r.relevance_score,` (relevanceScore now holds the cross-encoder score).
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:273-284 — `const CANONICAL_BOOST = 0.10; ... return { ...chunk, relevanceScore: Math.min(1.0, chunk.relevanceScore + CANONICAL_BOOST) }; ... termBoosted.sort((a, b) => b.relevanceScore - a.relevanceScore);`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:268-270 — `const queryTerms = canonicalTerms.filter(t => t.length >= 4 && queryLower.includes(t.toLowerCase()));` — substring, not word-boundary.
Corpus check: `corpus/index/compiled-index.json` carries 1,722 canonicalTerms, 1,709 of length ≥4, including 'care','soul','time','fear','form','being','world','place','light','sound','cause','style','voice','truth','logos','mood','talk','signs'.
findings.failure_scenario: Query "How does rhetorical incorporation operate in Red Dead Redemption 2" matches canonical terms {incorporation, rede, rhetoric} (measured). The reranker returns chunk A at 0.86 (the correct passage, does not contain the literal string) and chunk B at 0.79 (contains "rhetoric" in a bibliography line). B becomes min(1.0, 0.89) = 0.89 and is re-sorted above A. With scores near the ceiling — A=0.97, B=0.93 — both clamp to 1.0 and the top-K slice at :293 becomes arbitrary.
findings.consequence: A measured retrieval improvement is silently undone by an unvalidated heuristic applied downstream of it. Note also 'rede' matched via substring inside "Redemption" — the ≥4-char guard does not prevent substring collisions.
findings.fix_sketch: Move the boost BEFORE rerankResults so the cross-encoder has the final say, or make it a multiplicative prior on the *retrieval* score (`retrievalScore`) rather than an additive term on the rerank score, and require word-boundary matching (`new RegExp('\\b'+escape(t)+'\\b','i')`). ~20 lines. Then A/B it — the evaluation harness already exists per scripts/test-rerank-wiring.ts.

findings.claim: The knowledge-graph boost multiplies the post-rerank score by 1.2 / 1.1 / 1.05 and clamps to 1.0, then re-sorts. Same saturation pathology as the canonical boost, stacked on top of it.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:583-584 — `const KU_BOOST_FACTOR = 1.2; const KU_OVERLAP_THRESHOLD = 0.15;`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:598-603 — `if (bestOverlap >= KU_OVERLAP_THRESHOLD) { return { ...chunk, relevanceScore: Math.min(1.0, chunk.relevanceScore * KU_BOOST_FACTOR), }; }`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:641-642 — `const EDGE_BOOST_FACTOR = 1.1; const EDGE_HOP2_BOOST = 1.05;`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:701 — `boosted.sort((a, b) => b.relevanceScore - a.relevanceScore);`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:245-247 — kgBoosted runs on `reranked`, not on the raw retrieval scores.
retrieval-stage.ts:204-206 — `rerank: true, boostWithKG: true, maxHops: 2,` — every production write enables both.
setOverlap denominator is the *claim* word set (smart-retrieval-layer.ts:853-859), so a 6-word KU claim needs only 1 word present in a 450-3,000-char chunk to clear 0.15.
findings.failure_scenario: 588 KUs are loaded (god-learn/knowledge.jsonl = 588 lines). A KU claim "phantasia is a movement of the soul" tokenizes to {phantasia, movement, soul} after stopword filtering; any chunk containing "soul" hits 0.33 overlap and gets ×1.2. With rerank scores in the 0.85-0.99 band typical of bge-reranker-v2-m3, ×1.2 clamps essentially every soul-mentioning chunk to exactly 1.0, and the sort at :701 orders them by whatever the map produced.
findings.consequence: Two successive heuristic layers each capable of flattening the cross-encoder's discrimination to a plateau at 1.0. The three logged "Step 4b / Step 4c" lines report counts, never the score deltas, so the flattening is invisible in logs.
findings.fix_sketch: Same as the canonical boost: apply KG and term priors to `retrievalScore` and fuse with the rerank score via a documented combination (e.g. `final = rerank + w_kg*kgPrior + w_term*termPrior` with w tuned on the existing eval set), never by multiplying and clamping. ~30 lines plus a tuning run.

findings.claim: rerankResults returns only the chunks the reranker echoed back. If the rerank server applies any top_n, the missing chunks are silently dropped from retrieval — no length check, no log.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1234-1238 — the request body is `{ model: 'bge-reranker-v2-m3', query, documents: chunks.map((c) => c.content), }` — no `top_n` is sent, so the server's default governs.
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1255-1264 — `const reranked = results.filter((r) => Number.isInteger(r.index) && r.index >= 0 && r.index < chunks.length).map((r) => { ... });`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1266-1268 — `if (reranked.length === 0) { throw new Error('rerank indices did not map to any chunk'); }` — the ONLY length guard is against zero.
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1270-1272 logs `Rerank applied: ${reranked.length} chunks reordered` — a shrunken list reads as success.
findings.failure_scenario: poolSize is 30 (maxChunks 10 × candidateMultiplier 3, :926). The rerank service defaults top_n=10. 30 documents go in, 10 results come back, `reranked.length === 10`, and 20 candidates vanish before the diversity/limit stages. If the server instead returns duplicate indices, the same chunk is emitted twice and both survive to the LLM prompt.
findings.consequence: The widened candidate pool that rerank exists to exploit is silently truncated by the server, and the log line reports the truncated count as the reordered count. Also destroys the author-diversity ordering computed at :1116-1166 with no trace.
findings.fix_sketch: Send `top_n: chunks.length` explicitly; assert `reranked.length === chunks.length` and de-duplicate indices, warning (not throwing) and falling back to the input ordering on mismatch. ~10 lines.

findings.claim: Reranker degradation warns exactly once per process via a static flag and then returns unreranked results forever, while the endpoint defaults to a hardcoded LAN IP and rerank defaults to enabled. A wrong network produces a silently unreranked pipeline.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:70 — `private static rerankWarned = false;` (class-static: shared by every instance, never reset anywhere in the file).
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1276-1284 — `if (!SmartRetrievalLayer.rerankWarned) { SmartRetrievalLayer.rerankWarned = true; this.logger.warn(...`(Warned once per process.)`); } return chunks;`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1193-1199 — `return ( this.config.rerank?.endpoint || process.env.GOD_RERANK_ENDPOINT || 'http://192.168.50.22:8100/v1/rerank' );`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1186-1191 — `isRerankEnabled()` returns `true` by default.
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:242 — `this.logger.info(`[SmartRetrievalLayer] Step 4 after rerank: ${reranked.length}`);` — logs identically whether rerank succeeded or was skipped.
findings.failure_scenario: The pipeline runs on the MacBook Air or CHIMERA (per project memory, both are active dev boxes) where 192.168.50.22 is unreachable. The first retrieveContext emits one WARN. Every subsequent retrieval in that process silently returns cosine-ordered chunks while logging "Step 4 after rerank: 30". Meanwhile :924-928 still widened the pool to 30 because `rerankActive` only checks the *config* flag, not reachability — so 3× the chunks are fetched and none are reranked.
findings.consequence: The component the project's own evaluation identified as the retrieval win is silently absent on two of three machines, and the log line that should reveal it reports success. Combined with :926, a down reranker also silently changes what gets retrieved.
findings.fix_sketch: Make rerankWarned an instance field with a periodic re-warn (or a failure counter), gate `rerankActive` on a health probe result rather than the config flag, and add the rerank status to the returned pipelineHealth/corpusContextInfo so a drafting run records whether it was reranked. ~25 lines.

findings.claim: `retrievalQueries`, `subsections`, and `semanticQueries` are the SAME array object in the default (no explicit headings) path. The ontology query expansion mutates elements in place, so the document's section headings become "heading + injected Greek/German ontology terms."
findings.evidence:
retrieval-stage.ts:152 — `const semanticQueries = deps.extractSemanticRetrievalQueries(topic);`
retrieval-stage.ts:163 — `subsections = semanticQueries;` (assignment, not copy)
retrieval-stage.ts:167 — `const retrievalQueries = hasExplicitHeadings ? semanticQueries : subsections;`
retrieval-stage.ts:176-178 — `if (expansion.semanticTerms.length > 0) { retrievalQueries[i] = `${retrievalQueries[i]} ${expansion.semanticTerms.join(' ')}`; ... }`
retrieval-stage.ts:570 (buildResult) — `subsections: args.subsections,` is returned to the drafting stage as the outline.
retrieval-stage.ts:486 — `const constraintHeadings = hasExplicitHeadings ? subsections : deps.extractRetrievalQueries(topic);` — the constraint path re-derives, so headings and constraints now disagree.
findings.failure_scenario: Topic has no "Section N:" markers (the default). semanticQueries = ['world-disclosedness in VR', ...]. expandQueryWithOntology (corpus-index-provider.ts:166-198) matches the 'World' node and appends its transliteration. subsections[0] is now 'world-disclosedness in VR World Welt'. That string is emitted as a section heading in the generated document.
findings.consequence: Retrieval-internal query enrichment leaks into the rendered document structure. Only the `hasExplicitHeadings` branch is safe, because :157 builds a fresh array via `.map`.
findings.fix_sketch: `const retrievalQueries = [...(hasExplicitHeadings ? semanticQueries : subsections)];` — one line. Add a regression test asserting `subsections` is unchanged after the expansion block.

findings.claim: Exactly one ChromaDB collection — 'knowledge_chunks' — is reachable at runtime. No call site anywhere in the repo passes chromadb.collectionName or collectionId, so every other collection in vector_db_1536 is dead storage.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:87-92 — `chromadb: { host: 'localhost', port: 8001, collectionName: 'knowledge_chunks', ...config.chromadb, },`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:124 — `const collectionName = this.config.chromadb?.collectionName || 'knowledge_chunks';`
Construction sites, all zero-argument: express-server.ts:3938 `new SmartRetrievalLayer()`; lanham-write-test.ts:228; section-orchestrator.ts:464; universal-agent.ts:953; icp-api-routes.ts:99 and :1721; pdf-analysis-pipeline.ts:29.
`grep -rn "collectionName\|collectionId" src/` returns only smart-retrieval-layer.ts itself and an unrelated interfaces.ts:649.
vector_db_1536/ contains 6 collection UUID directories.
findings.failure_scenario: retrieval-stage.ts:190-198 pushes 'textual_analysis' and 'v2_knowledge_chunks' into `collections` when a Lanham signal is present, logs `Textual analysis collections added: textual_analysis, v2_knowledge_chunks`, and then queries 'knowledge_chunks' exactly as before. The log asserts something that did not happen.

(a) is ~10 lines and matches how the data is actually stored; (b) is ~60 lines. Do (a).

findings.claim: semanticSearch never reads options.minRelevance, so hybridSearch's `minRelevance: 0.6` is a no-op; but the merge then multiplies semantic scores by 0.7, and the caller filters at 0.6 — so hybrid search systematically discards chunks with cosine similarity below 0.857.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:873-877 — `private async semanticSearch(query: string, options: Partial<RetrievalOptions>): Promise<ContextChunk[]> { const maxChunks = options.maxChunks || this.DEFAULT_MAX_CHUNKS;` — the only field read besides `whereFilter` (:935) and `rerank` (:924). `minRelevance` never appears again in the method body (:873-1004).
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:353-356 — `this.semanticSearch(semanticQuery, { maxChunks: 20, minRelevance: 0.6, }),`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1321-1327 — `for (const chunk of semanticResults) { const weighted = { ...chunk, relevanceScore: chunk.relevanceScore * weights.semantic, }; ... }`
faceted-retrieval.ts:196-198 — `chunks = chunks.filter(c => c.relevanceScore >= minRelevance).slice(0, maxChunks);` with `minRelevance` defaulting to 0.6 (faceted-retrieval.ts:57).
findings.failure_scenario: A facet retrieves a chunk with cosine 0.82 (a strong match). keywordSearch returns non-empty, so mergeResults does not take the early-return at :1313-1315; the chunk becomes 0.82×0.7 = 0.574 and is filtered out at faceted-retrieval.ts:197 by the 0.6 threshold. Only chunks with cosine ≥ 0.857 survive.
findings.consequence: Facets silently starve. checkScarcity then fires 'low_span_count'/'single_document' warnings (faceted-retrieval.ts:500-532) that blame the corpus for a scoring bug. The 0.6 threshold means one thing to the caller (cosine) and another to the filter (weighted composite) — the same number, two scales.
findings.fix_sketch: Apply minRelevance inside semanticSearch (or in retrieveContext only, and stop passing it to semanticSearch), and normalise merged scores back to [0,1] before returning from hybridSearch so downstream thresholds compare like with like. ~10 lines.

findings.claim: If the Chroma response lacks a `distances` array, every chunk silently receives relevanceScore 1.0 — a perfect score for an unscored result. And the L2→cosine conversion assumes the collection was built with hnsw:space=l2 on unit-norm vectors; nothing checks.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:961 — `const distances = chromaResult.distances?.[0] || [];`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:969-970 — `const distance = distances[i] || 0;` then `const relevanceScore = Math.max(0, 1 - (distance * distance) / 2);` → distance 0 (or undefined) ⇒ score 1.0.
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:932 — `include: ['documents', 'metadatas', 'distances'],` — the request asks for distances, but the parse has no guard on the response actually containing them.
No code anywhere reads the collection's `hnsw:space` metadata.
findings.failure_scenario: A Chroma version change, an `include` rejection, or a partially-populated response yields `distances: [[]]`. All N chunks get relevanceScore 1.0. Every downstream threshold passes; boostDiversity's ordering is meaningless; the rerank pool is filled with whatever Chroma returned first; buildCorpusConstraint (minRelevance 0.0 at retrieval-stage.ts:495) admits all of them.
findings.consequence: Failure presents as maximally-confident retrieval rather than as an error. If the collection is cosine-space instead of l2, distances lie in [0,2] and the formula produces plausible-but-wrong scores across the board with no symptom at all.
findings.fix_sketch: `if (!Array.isArray(chromaResult.distances?.[0]) || chromaResult.distances[0].length !== ids.length) throw new Error(...)`, and read the collection's configured distance metric once during resolveCollectionId and select the conversion accordingly. ~15 lines.

findings.claim: QuoteSpan.clean_text_range and clean_range_hash are computed against the retrieved chunk's (possibly trimmed and collaged) text, and the hashed slice is the UNTRIMMED regex match while span.text is the TRIMMED one. The offsets cannot locate the quote in the source document and the hash cannot validate the span it accompanies.
findings.evidence:
faceted-retrieval.ts:246 — `const text = chunk.clean_text ?? chunk.content;` (`clean_text` does not exist on ContextChunk — tsc error TS2339 at 246,24 — so this is always `chunk.content`).
faceted-retrieval.ts:289-290 — `clean_text_range: [sentence.start, sentence.end], clean_range_hash: sha256(text.slice(sentence.start, sentence.end)),`
faceted-retrieval.ts:321-328 — `while ((match = sentencePattern.exec(text)) !== null) { const sentenceText = match[0].trim(); if (sentenceText.length >= 20) { results.push({ text: sentenceText, start: match.index, end: match.index + match[0].length, }); } }` — `text` is trimmed, `[start,end]` spans the untrimmed match including its trailing `\s+`.
faceted-retrieval.ts:293 — `text: sentence.text,` (the trimmed form).
icp-types.ts:331-334 — the field contract is "Range in clean_text [start, end]" / "Hash of clean_text at this range (for staleness detection)".
findings.failure_scenario: retrieval-stage.ts:319 has already replaced chunk.content with a 450-char collage of non-adjacent sentences. A span at [120,187] of the collage corresponds to nothing at [120,187] of the source document. Independently, `sha256(text.slice(start,end))` hashes "…theory. " (with trailing space) while span.text is "…theory." — so recomputing the hash from span.text never matches, and staleness detection reports every span as stale.
findings.consequence: The claim/clause-level provenance layer — the exact capability the user wants to scale — records offsets and hashes that are structurally incapable of pointing back at the document. Every quote-span verification built on these fields is verifying a derivative artifact.
findings.fix_sketch: Carry an immutable `sourceText` (or doc_id + character offset into the ingested clean text) on ContextChunk alongside the display-trimmed content, compute spans against it, and hash exactly `sentence.text`. Requires ContextChunk to gain `clean_text`/`source_kind` for real (they are currently phantom reads) and requires retrieval-stage to stop mutating `content`. ~60-100 lines across three files.

findings.claim: validateCitation treats any 1-3 digit number as "probably a page number, which is fine" and never checks it against the source's page ranges, while matching authors by two-way substring. MLA parentheticals — the project's mandated citation style — are therefore validated against author surname fragments alone.
findings.evidence:
corpus-constraint-builder.ts:295 — `const authorYearMatch = normalized.match(/([a-z']+)[,\s]+(\d{4}|\d+)/i);`
corpus-constraint-builder.ts:307 — `if (sourceLastName.includes(authorPart) || authorPart.includes(sourceLastName)) {`
corpus-constraint-builder.ts:313-316 — `} else { // It's probably a page number, which is fine\n  return { valid: true, matchedSource: source }; }`
corpus-constraint-builder.ts:103 — the constraint DOES carry the real page ranges: `pages: mergedPages.length > 0 ? formatPageRanges(mergedPages) : undefined,` — and validateCitation never reads `source.pages`.
findings.failure_scenario: The model emits "(Barrett 4711)" for a 300-page book. normalized → authorPart 'barrett', yearOrPage '4711' (length 4 → treated as a YEAR, compared to source.year, fails) — but "(Barrett 471)" (length 3) takes the page branch and returns valid:true unconditionally. Separately, "(Be 12)" → authorPart 'be' → `'bernstein'.includes('be')` → valid. Non-ASCII surnames break the parse entirely: 'uexküll 1934' backtracks to authorPart 'll', which then substring-matches 'uexküll'.
findings.consequence: Fabricated page numbers pass citation validation in a project whose memory records citation rigor as UTMOST PRIORITY. The correct data to validate against is computed 200 lines earlier and discarded.
findings.fix_sketch: Parse MLA `(Surname NN)` explicitly, require a minimum author-fragment length (≥3) and a *prefix* match rather than two-way substring, and validate the page against `source.pages` by expanding the merged ranges. Add `\p{L}` Unicode classes for non-ASCII surnames. ~40 lines.

findings.claim: Manifest-derived additional sources are de-duplicated on author+year ONLY, ignoring title. A second work by the same author in the same year is silently excluded from the citation whitelist.
findings.failure_scenario: A chunk from Heidegger 1927 *Sein und Zeit* is retrieved. The manifest also carries Heidegger 1927 *Die Grundprobleme der Phänomenologie*. `exists` is true on author+year, so Grundprobleme never enters `sources`. The drafting stage receives a whitelist without it; any citation to it is later classified as hallucinated by the citation enforcer.
findings.consequence: Correct, corpus-backed citations are flagged as hallucinations, and the model is steered away from a work that IS in the corpus. Common for prolific authors — precisely the dissertation's core authors.
findings.fix_sketch: Include title in the `exists` predicate, matching the two other de-duplication keys in the same file. One line.

findings.claim: Seven of the eight failure paths in the retrieval stage call recordWarning, which is EXCLUDED from computePipelineHealth. Two swallow entirely. A run in which every sub-query failed reports pipelineHealth 'clean'.
findings.evidence:
stage-types.ts:63-67 — `export function computePipelineHealth(ctx: PipelineContext): PipelineHealth {\n  if (ctx.hardFailures.length > 0) return 'failed';\n  if (ctx.degradedEvents.length > 0) return 'degraded';\n  return 'clean';\n}` — `ctx.warnings` is never consulted.
stage-types.ts:88-91 — `recordWarning` pushes to `ctx.warnings` and logs at `info` level.
retrieval-stage.ts:241 — `recordWarning(ctx, 'retrieval', `Sub-query failed for "${sq}": ${e}`);`
retrieval-stage.ts:271, :290, :351 — the same for author supplementation, title retrieval, coverage supplementation.
retrieval-stage.ts:439, :465, :482 — the same for KU loading, edge loading, corpus index loading.
retrieval-stage.ts:184 — `} catch { /* query expansion is non-critical */ }` — no record at all.
retrieval-stage.ts:310 — `} catch { /* non-critical */ }` — no record at all.
write-pipeline-orchestrator.ts:3996, :4029 — `const pipelineHealth = computePipelineHealth(ctx);` … `pipelineHealth,` is the value returned to the caller.
findings.failure_scenario: ChromaDB is up but the embedding API on :8000 is down. Every retrieveContext returns [] (semanticSearch swallows at :904-908). No exception is thrown, so not even recordWarning fires. corpusChunks is empty, the else-branch at :498-503 builds a constraint from the manifest, and the run returns pipelineHealth 'clean' with corpusContext.used === false buried in the result object.
findings.consequence: There is no signal at any level — no exit code, no health flag, no error counter — that distinguishes "retrieved 28 grounded chunks" from "retrieved nothing and drafted from the model's parametric memory."
findings.fix_sketch: Promote retrieval sub-query failures to recordDegraded, add `if (ctx.warnings.length > threshold) return 'degraded'` to computePipelineHealth, and add a hard assertion in the retrieval stage: if whitelistMode is on and corpusChunks.length === 0, recordHardFailure. ~15 lines.

findings.claim: Keyword-expansion chunks have their relevanceScore overwritten with a fabricated constant 0.85, which then drives diversity enforcement, attention reordering and constraint building as if it were a measured score.
findings.failure_scenario: A Greek ontology keyword like 'φαντασία' retrieves 3 chunks at true cosine 0.42/0.39/0.31. All three are stamped 0.85 and, being above nearly everything else, are placed in the high-attention head positions by reorderChunksForAttention. Weak matches are presented to the model as the strongest evidence.
findings.consequence: Score fabrication propagates into every ranking decision downstream. Note the guard uses the broken `undefined:page` id, so the stamping is also applied non-deterministically depending on page-number collisions.
findings.fix_sketch: Carry a separate `expansionBoost` flag or set `retrievalScore` and apply a bounded additive prior rather than overwriting the measured score. ~5 lines.

findings.claim: boostDiversity's author cap runs BEFORE the reranker and only reorders (it never drops), so the reranker immediately re-sorts and the author cap has no effect on what the maxChunks slice keeps.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1121-1138 — `const maxPerAuthor = Math.max(Math.ceil(chunks.length * 0.3), 3); ... for (const chunk of chunks) { ... if (count < maxPerAuthor) { authorCapped.push(chunk); ... } else { overflow.push(chunk); } } const combined = [...authorCapped, ...overflow];` — overflow is appended, not dropped.
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:233-241 — `const diverse = opts.diversityBoost ? this.boostDiversity(filtered) : filtered;` then `const reranked = opts.rerank ? await this.rerankResults(query, diverse) : diverse;`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1255-1264 — rerankResults rebuilds the list in the reranker's order, discarding the author-capped order entirely.
retrieval-stage.ts:200-206 sets both `diversityBoost: true` and `rerank: true`.
findings.failure_scenario: A 30-chunk pool is 22 Heidegger + 8 others. boostDiversity puts 9 Heidegger first, then the 8 others, then 13 Heidegger. The reranker re-sorts by cross-encoder score and returns 18 Heidegger in the top 20. `.slice(0, maxChunks)` at :293 keeps 9 Heidegger and 1 other.
findings.consequence: The author-domination guard is inert in the only configuration production uses. enforceSourceDiversity at retrieval-stage.ts:315 partially compensates but with a different cap (8 per source) and only after the per-query slice has already discarded the alternatives.
findings.fix_sketch: Apply the author cap AFTER rerank and before the maxChunks slice, or make boostDiversity actually drop overflow instead of appending it. ~10 lines.

findings.claim: loadProtectedTerms is a second, independent, per-instance cache of compiled-index.json with no mtime check and no invalidation. It also negative-caches: if the index is missing or malformed on first call, an empty Set is memoised for the process lifetime.
findings.failure_scenario: The observability daemon starts before `scripts/compile-corpus-index.py` has run. protectedTerms is memoised empty. After the index is compiled, tokenize (:835, :841) continues to strip 'being', 'care', 'time' and every other ontology term that collides with STOPWORDS, for the life of the daemon. The C-03 fix the code documents at :792 is silently disabled.
findings.consequence: KG boosting quality degrades permanently and invisibly after any index rebuild or any process that starts before the index exists. jsonl-loaders' mtime cache correctly picks up rebuilds; this one does not.
findings.fix_sketch: Delegate to `loadCompiledIndex()` from jsonl-loaders.ts (which already mtime-invalidates) and derive protectedTerms from its result, memoised on the same mtime. ~10 lines, and removes one of three redundant parses of a 664 KB file.

findings.claim: hybridSearch's cache key omits the (dropped) options argument, so N concurrent per-collection calls share one key, all miss simultaneously, and all issue duplicate embedding + Chroma round-trips. There is no in-flight request de-duplication anywhere in the class.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:337-341 — `const cacheKey = this.buildCacheKey(
  'hybrid',
  `${semanticQuery}|${keywords.join(',')}`,
  weights
);`
faceted-retrieval.ts:151-170 — `const retrievalPromises = collections.map(async (collection) => { ... hybridSearch(query, retrievalTerms, {semantic:0.7,keyword:0.3}, {...}) ... }); const allResults = await Promise.all(retrievalPromises);`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1436-1465 — setCache has no pending-promise map.
findings.failure_scenario: A facet with 5 collections fires 5 concurrent hybridSearch calls with identical (query, keywords, weights). All 5 read an empty cache, all 5 embed the same query on the GPU box and all 5 query Chroma, then all 5 write the same entry. Under the retrieveContext path, section-orchestrator.ts:576 does the same with 3 collections (there the keys differ because `collections` IS in the key at :208, guaranteeing 3 identical searches with no cache benefit at all).
findings.consequence: 3-5× wasted embedding/Chroma load per facet or section, scaling linearly with the collection count. At 100× corpus volume with more facets this becomes the dominant cost.
findings.fix_sketch: Add a `Map<string, Promise<ContextChunk[]>>` of in-flight requests keyed the same way, resolved into the LRU on completion. ~20 lines, and it also fixes the retrieveContext path.

findings.claim: KG boosting is three nested linear scans over the full KU and edge sets with no index. Today that is 588 KUs and 5,437 edges; the user's target is claim-level records at ~100× volume.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:586-596 — `const boosted = chunks.map((chunk) => { const chunkWords = this.tokenize(chunk.content); ... for (const ku of kus) { const claimWords = ku._claimWords!; const overlap = this.setOverlap(chunkWords, claimWords); ... } ... });`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:618-623 — `for (const edge of edges) { ... }` (full scan).
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:627-638 — `for (const concept of topicConcepts) { for (const edge of edges) { ... } }`.
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:666-677 — `for (const concept of expansionConcepts) { for (const edge of edges) { ... } }`.
`wc -l god-learn/knowledge.jsonl god-reason/reasoning.jsonl` → 588 / 5,437.
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:645-656 and :681-692 — `for (let i = 0; i < boosted.length; i++) { const chunkLower = boosted[i].content.toLowerCase(); for (const concept of ...) { if (chunkLower.includes(concept)) ...` — a fresh `.toLowerCase()` of every chunk inside the outer loop, done twice.
findings.failure_scenario: Today, per retrieveContext call: 30 chunks × 588 KUs = 17,640 set intersections, plus 5,437 + |topicConcepts|×5,437 + |expansionConcepts|×5,437 edge iterations. With 20 topic concepts and 200 expansion concepts that is ~1.2M iterations per query, and retrieval-stage issues 8-15 queries per draft. At 100× (58,800 KUs, 543,700 edges) it becomes ~120M iterations per query — tens of seconds of single-threaded JS per sub-query.
findings.consequence: The KG-boost stage is the hard scalability wall for the stated goal. It is also loaded entirely into process memory (`this.kgKUs`, `this.kgEdges`, :60-61) — 100× of 5,437 JSON edge objects is a multi-GB resident set.
findings.fix_sketch: Invert to precomputed indices: a term→KU-ids inverted index and a concept→edge adjacency map, both built once per mtime generation and stored on disk (or in SQLite/the existing AgentDB) rather than as JS arrays. The boost then becomes O(chunk terms) lookups. ~200-300 lines, and it is the single highest-leverage change for the 100× goal.

findings.claim: The candidate pool is hard-capped at 50 chunks per query regardless of configuration, so no amount of corpus growth or maxChunks increase can widen recall.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:924-928 — `const rerankActive = options.rerank === true && this.isRerankEnabled();
  const poolSize = rerankActive
    ? Math.min(maxChunks * this.rerankCandidateMultiplier(), 50)
    : maxChunks * 2;`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:931 — `n_results: poolSize, // widened to candidateMultiplier×maxChunks (≤50) when reranking`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:1205-1207 — `return this.config.rerank?.candidateMultiplier ?? 3;` — configurable, but the 50 is a literal.
findings.failure_scenario: maxChunks is raised to 40 for a comprehensive section. rerankActive is true, so poolSize = min(120, 50) = 50. The reranker sees 50 candidates and the pipeline requests 40 — a 1.25× pool where the code intends 3×. The `rerankCandidateMultiplier` config knob is silently overridden.
findings.consequence: Recall is capped by a magic number that is invisible to configuration. Note also the asymmetry: with rerank OFF the pool is `maxChunks * 2` = 80, i.e. LARGER than with rerank on — enabling the reranker can shrink the candidate pool.
findings.fix_sketch: Make the cap a config field (`rerank.maxCandidatePool`) and take `Math.max(maxChunks * 2, min(maxChunks * multiplier, cap))` so enabling rerank never narrows the pool. ~4 lines.

findings.claim: The documented "Final fallback: basic semantic search" can never execute, because hybridSearch swallows all its own errors and returns [] rather than throwing.
findings.failure_scenario: ChromaDB is down. hybridSearch logs and returns []. The catch never fires. `chunks` is [], and the facet reports 'low_span_count' scarcity (faceted-retrieval.ts:500-506) rather than falling back. The same dead-catch pattern appears at :165-168 in the per-collection branch.
findings.consequence: The intended resilience path is unreachable; the failure surfaces as an evidence-scarcity warning about the corpus rather than an infrastructure error. This is also the reason the ICP faceted path never reranks: the reachable path is hybridSearch (no rerank at all), and the unreachable fallback is the only one that calls retrieveContext — and even that omits `rerank: true`.
findings.fix_sketch: Have hybridSearch rethrow infrastructure errors (matching retrieveContext's F-13 policy at :306-313), and add `rerank: true` to the fallback. ~6 lines.

findings.claim: verification_status is hardcoded to 'flagged' at construction, so FacetCoverage.verified_span_count is structurally always 0 and can never inform scarcity decisions.
findings.evidence:
faceted-retrieval.ts:296 — `verification_status: 'flagged',` — the only assignment in the file.
faceted-retrieval.ts:471-475 — `const verified = spans.filter(s =>
  s.verification_status === 'auto_verified' ||
  s.verification_status === 'human_verified' ||
  s.verification_status === 'human_corrected',
);`
faceted-retrieval.ts:484 — `verified_span_count: verified.length,`
faceted-retrieval.ts:509-532 — checkScarcity never reads `coverage.verified_span_count`.
findings.failure_scenario: Any call. verified.length is 0 for every facet, always.
findings.consequence: A coverage metric that is reported to the ICP UI and to downstream consumers as if it measured something. It measures nothing.
findings.fix_sketch: Either populate verification_status from the verification stage before computeCoverage runs, or delete the field from FacetCoverage. ~5 lines either way; the point is that the current state is a silent lie in a provenance-critical structure.

findings.claim: Two phantom property reads on ContextChunk: `clean_text` and `source_kind` do not exist on the type or at runtime, so sourceKind is the constant 'CORPUS' and the entire EXTERNAL branch of SourceAdmissionPolicy is unreachable.
findings.evidence:
faceted-retrieval.ts:246-247 — `const text = chunk.clean_text ?? chunk.content;\n  const sourceKind: SourceKind = chunk.source_kind ?? 'CORPUS';`
tsc: `src/god-agent/retrieval/faceted-retrieval.ts(246,24): error TS2339: Property 'clean_text' does not exist on type 'ContextChunk'.` and `(247,42): error TS2339: Property 'source_kind' does not exist on type 'ContextChunk'.`
retrieval/types.ts:136-181 — ContextChunk declares chunkId, docId, content, metadata, relevanceScore, retrievalScore, embedding. Neither clean_text nor source_kind is present, and the index signature at :170 is on `metadata`, not on the chunk itself.
faceted-retrieval.ts:441-450 — `const rules = policy.candidate_rules.filter(r => r.source_kind === span.source_kind && ...); if (rules.length === 0) { if (span.source_kind === 'CORPUS') return true; ... }`
findings.failure_scenario: An admission policy defines EXTERNAL rules with min_authority_tier. No span ever has source_kind 'EXTERNAL', so those rules match nothing and the `rules.length === 0` branch unconditionally admits every span via the CORPUS shortcut.
findings.consequence: The two-phase SourceAdmissionPolicy the module's docstring describes (:5-7) degenerates to "admit everything" for the only source kind that can occur. Runs fine under tsx; only tsc sees it.
findings.fix_sketch: Add `clean_text?: string` and `source_kind?: SourceKind` to ContextChunk and populate them in semanticSearch from metadata, or read them from `chunk.metadata` (which does have the index signature). ~8 lines — but note the fix must not paper over the fact that nothing currently sets these values.

findings.claim: isRelevantToFacet is defined and never called — the facet-relevance filter it implements was removed from the extraction loop and the method left behind.
findings.failure_scenario: N/A — the consequence is volume, not incorrectness: every sentence ≥20 chars in every retrieved chunk becomes a QuoteSpan with a randomUUID, three SHA-256 hashes and a provenance scorecard.
findings.consequence: With maxChunksPerFacet 15 and 450-3,000-char chunks, that is on the order of 100-400 spans per facet, each carrying 3 hashes. At 100× corpus volume with claim-level facets this is the memory and hashing hot spot. Also `retrievalTerms` is now an unused parameter of extractSpansFromChunk.
findings.fix_sketch: Delete the method and the unused parameter, or reinstate it as an opt-in pre-filter behind a config flag. ~5 lines.

findings.claim: keywordSearch silently drops all but the first three keywords and uses ChromaDB's case-SENSITIVE `$contains`, while scoring against lowercased content — so scores are computed on a different match criterion than the retrieval.
findings.failure_scenario: A facet supplies retrieval_lexicon ['Phantasia','aisthesis','nous','hexis','energeia','entelecheia']. Only the first three are searched; 'Phantasia' capitalised matches no lowercase occurrence in the corpus; the score denominator is 6 (all keywords) while at most 3 could ever contribute, so scores are capped at 0.5 — below the 0.6 default threshold at faceted-retrieval.ts:57.
findings.consequence: Keyword search structurally cannot produce a score high enough to survive the caller's own threshold when more than ~3-4 keywords are supplied. Combined with mergeResults' early-return at :1313-1315 (empty keyword results ⇒ semantic results pass through unweighted), the "hybrid" in hybridSearch is usually not hybrid at all.
findings.fix_sketch: Search all keywords (or make the cap configurable), lowercase both sides or use a case-insensitive Chroma operator, and use the number of *searched* keywords as the denominator. Log non-ok responses. ~15 lines.

findings.claim: The word 'collections' denotes three different things across the pipeline — ChromaDB collection names, manifest `collection` field values, and corpus folder paths — and the augmented list built at :189-198 is used for the (inert) retrieval call but NOT for the manifest load, which reads the un-augmented option.
findings.failure_scenario: A user passes `--corpus-collections rhetorical_ontology`. The manifest loader correctly filters (metadata semantics). The retrieval layer ignores it entirely (Chroma semantics, unread). The resulting CorpusConstraint whitelist is narrow while the retrieved chunks are corpus-wide — so chunks from outside the whitelist are handed to the model and every citation to them is flagged hallucinated.
findings.consequence: A single overloaded name causes the citation whitelist and the retrieved evidence to be scoped by different rules. The user-visible `corpusContext.collections` report is a third, unrelated value.
findings.fix_sketch: Rename to three distinct fields — `chromaCollections`, `manifestCollections`, `corpusFolders` — and make retrieval-stage pass the same effective list to both the retrieval call and the manifest load. ~30 lines of mechanical renaming across ~15 sites, plus the `$in` filter implementation from finding 4.

findings.claim: buildCacheKey's docstring promises sorted keys for deterministic cache hits; the implementation does not sort. Two option objects with identical semantics but different property order produce different cache keys.
findings.failure_scenario: retrieval-stage.ts:261 spreads `{...retrievalOpts, maxChunks: 16, whereFilter: {...}}` and :340 spreads `{...retrievalOpts, maxChunks: 8, whereFilter: {...}}`. Property order happens to be stable today because opts is rebuilt literally at :193-205. Any future caller constructing options differently — or a whereFilter built by iterating a Map — silently bypasses the cache.
findings.consequence: Latent: correct today by accident of construction order, and the comment asserts a guarantee the code does not provide. It also means the cache key embeds the *inert* `collections` field, which is why section-orchestrator's three identical searches each get their own cache slot.
findings.fix_sketch: `JSON.stringify(options, Object.keys(options).sort())` loses nested objects (as the comment correctly warns); use a small recursive canonical-stringify instead. ~12 lines.

findings.claim: The "LRU" cache does a full O(n) linear scan of up to 1,000 entries on every insert once at capacity, and entries are never evicted by corpus change — only by TTL or capacity.
findings.failure_scenario: A long-running daemon fills the cache to 1,000. Every subsequent retrieval walks all 1,000 entries to find the LRU victim. Meanwhile a corpus re-ingest changes the underlying chunks; nothing invalidates, so up to 30 minutes of drafting runs against stale content.
findings.consequence: Memory growth plus O(n) insert cost, and — more importantly for this project — a retrieval cache with no coupling to the ingest that produces its contents. `getCacheStats` at :526-547 also mislabels: `hitRate` is computed as `entries with accessCount > 1 / cache.size`, which is not a hit rate.
findings.fix_sketch: Use a real LRU (Map insertion-order re-set on access gives O(1) eviction in ~6 lines), and stamp each entry with the ingest generation / manifest mtime so a re-ingest invalidates. ~25 lines.

findings.claim: Four TODO stubs are wired into public API paths: getRelatedChunks can never return anything, the pageContext option is a silent no-op, and findCrossReferences' "semantic similarity" is Jaccard word overlap.
findings.failure_scenario: Any call to getRelatedChunks(id, {direction:'both', count:2}) logs `SmartRetrievalLayer.getRelatedChunks error: Error: Chunk not found: <id>` and returns []. Any call to retrieveContext with pageContext > 0 gets exactly the un-expanded chunks with no indication the option was ignored.
findings.consequence: The three functions the module docstring advertises at :9-10 ("getRelatedChunks(): Expand context with surrounding chunks", "findCrossReferences(): Cross-document concept analysis") are non-functional or heuristic. For the stated goal — "every point of connection" — cross-document connection detection is currently word-overlap Jaccard with a 0.7 threshold (:481) and a similarity→relationship mapping (:1371-1375) that can only ever emit 'agrees'/'extends'/'related', never 'contradicts' or 'cites'.
findings.fix_sketch: getChunkById/getChunksByRange are ~20 lines each against the Chroma `get` endpoint using the `{doc_id}:{idx:05d}` id scheme the ingest already writes. computeSimilarity should reuse the embedding API. Contradiction detection needs an NLI model — that is a real project, not a patch.

findings.claim: RetrievalStats and RetrievalDirection are imported and never referenced.
findings.evidence: smart-retrieval-layer.ts:24-40 imports `RetrievalStats,` (:29) and `RetrievalDirection,` (:32). `grep -c RetrievalStats` and `grep -c RetrievalDirection` on the file both return 1 — the import line itself. No `RetrievalStats` object is ever constructed, so the module never reports queryTimeMs, cacheHit, or rerankTimeMs despite `const startTime = Date.now();` at :190 (also never read).
findings.failure_scenario: N/A.
findings.consequence: There is no instrumentation of retrieval latency, cache hit rate, or rerank cost anywhere in the layer, despite the types existing for it. `startTime` at :190 is assigned and never used — the timing was intended and dropped.
findings.fix_sketch: Either populate and emit RetrievalStats (~15 lines, and it would have made findings 6, 10 and 14 visible in logs) or delete the imports.

findings.claim: canonicalTerms contains 101 case-duplicate groups, so the boost's filter iterates ~6% redundant entries; the ordering instability the compiler introduces is harmless here but the duplication is real and measurable.
findings.evidence:
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:261 — `const canonicalTerms: string[] = (index as any).canonicalTerms;`
smart-retrieval-layer.ts:268-270 — `const queryTerms = canonicalTerms.filter(t => t.length >= 4 && queryLower.includes(t.toLowerCase()));`

findings.claim: The query is expanded twice by two functions with incompatible matching semantics — word-boundary regex in one, raw substring in the other — and the second expansion operates on the already-expanded string.

findings.failure_scenario: The substring form matches 'Form' inside 'information', 'Sein' inside 'Dasein', 'Rede' inside 'Redemption' (all are real node names or canonical terms in the working-tree index — 126 ontology node names are 4-8 chars, including 'Form','Care','Time','Soul','Signs','World','Truth'). Each spurious match appends that node's Greek, transliteration, translation and all aliases to the embedded query, diluting the query vector.

findings.fix_sketch: Use word-boundary matching in expandQueryWithCanonicalTerms to match the other expander, cap the number of appended terms (e.g. 8), and pick ONE expansion point rather than two. ~20 lines.

findings.claim: mergeResults returns unweighted results whenever either input is empty, so the hybrid weights silently do not apply — and given the keywordSearch defects above, the empty-keyword case is the common one.
findings.failure_scenario: keywordSearch returns [] (case-sensitive `$contains` miss, or all keywords <3 chars, or a swallowed HTTP error at :1039). hybridSearch returns pure semantic results at full cosine. The caller's 0.6 threshold now filters on cosine rather than on the weighted composite — a different, incompatible scale from the non-empty case.
findings.consequence: The same threshold value means two different things depending on whether keyword search happened to return anything. The comment documents this as a fix, but it is a scale discontinuity: the identical query can produce systematically higher or lower scores depending on an unrelated keyword-search outcome.
findings.fix_sketch: Normalise: always divide the merged score by the sum of the weights that actually contributed, so the output is on a consistent [0,1] scale regardless of which branch ran. ~6 lines.

**tsc result, as requested.** `npx tsc --noEmit 2>&1 | wc -l` = 179 lines; `grep -c "error TS"` = **exactly 157 errors** (the 22-line difference is multi-line type expansions). Worst offenders: section-orchestrator.ts (26), __experimental__/enhanced-quality-integration.ts (16), context-tier-manager.ts (13). **Four are in index code, all in faceted-retrieval.ts**: `(158,13)` and `(190,11)` TS2554 "Expected 2-3 arguments, but got 4" — the hybridSearch arity bug; `(246,24)` and `(247,42)` TS2339 — `clean_text` and `source_kind` do not exist on ContextChunk. smart-retrieval-layer.ts, retrieval-stage.ts and corpus-constraint-builder.ts produce **zero** errors, which is exactly why their defects are all runtime-invisible. Everything runs via `npx tsx` (package.json:25-39, transpile-only); `"typecheck": "tsc --noEmit"` exists at package.json:23 and is on no run path, no CI gate, no pre-commit hook.

**The three index touch points, precisely.** (1) *Query expansion before embedding*: retrieval-stage.ts:175 calls `expandQueryWithOntology` (word-boundary regex, corpus-index-provider.ts:180-183) and mutates `retrievalQueries[i]` in place at :177; smart-retrieval-layer.ts:888 then calls `expandQueryWithCanonicalTerms` (raw substring, cross-author-utils.ts:576-578) on the already-expanded string. Two expansions, two incompatible matching semantics, no cap on appended terms. Measured: a 62-char query becomes 162 chars with 8 appended terms. (2) *The +0.10 post-rerank boost* at :252-291: `Math.min(1.0, chunk.relevanceScore + 0.10)` applied to what is, after :1262, the cross-encoder score, then re-sorted at :284. (3) *The rerank call* at :239-241. Order is rerank → KG boost (×1.2/×1.1/×1.05, all clamped, re-sorted at :701) → term boost (+0.10, clamped, re-sorted). **The reranker — which the project's own evaluation identified as the retrieval win — is applied first and then overwritten twice by unvalidated heuristics that saturate at 1.0.**

**Second cache confirmed.** `loadProtectedTerms` at :794-818 is a per-instance cache with no mtime check and no reset, doing its own `readFileSync` + `JSON.parse` of the 664 KB compiled-index.json at :798-800, bypassing the mtime-invalidating shared loader. Worse than the prior claim: :796 assigns the empty Set *before* the existsSync guard at :799, so a missing index negative-caches empty for the process lifetime.

**RetrievalOptions.collections, end to end.** Written at retrieval-stage.ts:189-198, faceted-retrieval.ts:161 and :190-194, section-orchestrator.ts:580, smart-retrieval-layer.ts:452 and :463. Read at exactly one place: smart-retrieval-layer.ts:194, where it is copied into `opts` and never touched again. It is absent from the Chroma request body (:929-939). Consequences are wrong output, not missing output: `findCrossReferences` runs two identical unscoped searches and reports that source and target documents "agree"; section-orchestrator's three-way "multi-source retrieval" is one query executed three times and bucketed as notes/theory/empirical. The semantic collision is **three**-way, not two: Chroma collection names (retrieval-stage.ts:191), manifest `collection` metadata values (corpus-constraint-builder.ts:251-252), and corpus folder paths (icp-api-routes.ts:638). And it is moot anyway — no call site sets `chromadb.collectionName`/`collectionId`, so only `knowledge_chunks` is ever queried.

**hybridSearch.** Confirmed: no rerank path (rerankResults is called only from retrieveContext:240), hardcoded `{maxChunks:20, minRelevance:0.6}` at :353-356, `.slice(0, DEFAULT_MAX_CHUNKS)` = 10 at :369 regardless of caller. Both prior line references belong to **smart-retrieval-layer.ts, not faceted-retrieval.ts**. New: the `minRelevance: 0.6` is *inert* — semanticSearch never reads options.minRelevance anywhere in :873-1004 — while the merge multiplies semantic scores by 0.7 and the caller filters at 0.6, so hybrid search silently discards everything below cosine 0.857.

**The biggest finding is not on your list.** `retrieval-stage.ts:226` (and 19 sibling sites) computes the de-duplication key as `c.metadata.chunk_id || \`${c.metadata.source_id}:${c.metadata.page_start}\``. Neither field is ever written — not by semanticSearch (:972-990) and not by the ingest (run_ingest_phase2.py:1737-1753). The key is literally `"undefined:<page_start>"`, so the pipeline de-duplicates the entire corpus **by page number across all authors and all works**. Heidegger p.145 and Aristotle p.145 collide; the second is dropped with no log. The correct identifier — `chunkId` — is already on the object at :973. This is a ~20-line fix with more impact than every tuning change in the file.

**Second biggest.** retrieval-stage.ts:319 mutates `chunk.content` in place with `trimChunkContent`, which (retrieval-utils.ts:352-370) does not truncate — it score-ranks sentences, keeps the best ~450 chars, restores document order, and joins with a single space. The result is a **non-contiguous collage presented as continuous prose with no elision marker**, and because retrieveContext caches the very objects it returns (:303/:305/:1430), the mutation writes through into the 30-minute cache. This manufactures fabricated verbatim quotes that no downstream fidelity check can catch, since the collage *is* the chunk they validate against — in a project whose memory records citation rigor as UTMOST PRIORITY.

architecture_assessment.current_capability:
What this code does today, traced rather than described: it embeds a query (after two rounds of string-concatenation expansion), sends one vector to one ChromaDB collection named `knowledge_chunks`, converts L2 distance to cosine with an unverified formula, filters on a threshold that production sets to 0.0 (retrieval-stage.ts:202) or forces to 0.0 whenever a whereFilter is present (:196-198), reorders for author diversity in a way rerank immediately undoes, optionally reranks with a cross-encoder at a hardcoded LAN IP, then overwrites the rerank scores with two clamped heuristic boosts, slices to maxChunks, and returns object references it also stores in a 30-minute cache that the caller then mutates.

The index's role is decorative. It contributes (a) expansion strings appended to the query before embedding, (b) a +0.10 additive nudge on chunks that contain a matching substring, (c) a stopword-exemption whitelist, and (d) `ontologyLines`/`hookLines`/`tensionLines` that go into the PROMPT, never into chunk selection. Not one line of code uses the index to select, rank, or filter a chunk. The prior claim that the index carries "ontology CONCEPT NAMES and little else into runtime" is precisely right, and the reason is structural: the compiled index stores no chunk identifiers at all — `ontologyNodes` carry `units: string[]`, not doc_ids or chunk_ids — so it *cannot* address the corpus even if the code wanted to.

The retrieval unit is the chunk. There is no claim record, no clause record, no span record that survives retrieval. QuoteSpan (faceted-retrieval.ts:282-298) is the only clause-level structure and it is generated per-request, thrown away after the facet, and its `clean_text_range`/`clean_range_hash` are computed against a possibly-trimmed, possibly-collaged chunk body rather than the source document — so they cannot locate anything.
architecture_assessment.ceiling:
Concrete numbers, all measured on the working tree.

**Retrieval breadth: 50.** smart-retrieval-layer.ts:926 caps the candidate pool at `Math.min(maxChunks * 3, 50)`. No configuration can exceed it. Perversely, with rerank OFF the pool is `maxChunks * 2` = up to 80, so enabling the reranker can *narrow* the pool.

**Effective corpus reachable: one collection.** 6 collection directories exist under vector_db_1536/; exactly one is queryable, because all 7 `new SmartRetrievalLayer()` sites pass no config (:90, :124).

**Chunks per draft: bounded by distinct page numbers, not by chunk count.** The `undefined:<page_start>` de-duplication key means the union across 8-15 sub-queries is capped at the number of distinct `page_start` integers observed. targetChunks is 28 (gold-standard-config.ts:13); the practical ceiling is lower and depends on page-number collisions, which get *worse* as the corpus grows because more works share low page numbers.

**KG boost: O(chunks x KUs) + O(concepts x edges), pure linear scan.** Today 588 KUs (god-learn/knowledge.jsonl) and 5,437 edges (god-reason/reasoning.jsonl). Per retrieveContext call at pool 30: 17,640 set intersections, plus `5,437 + |topicConcepts| x 5,437 + |expansionConcepts| x 5,437` edge iterations (smart-retrieval-layer.ts:618-638, :664-677). With 20 topic and 200 expansion concepts that is ~1.2M iterations, times 8-15 sub-queries per draft. At 100x (58,800 KUs, 543,700 edges) it is ~120M iterations per sub-query — tens of seconds of single-threaded JS each — and both arrays are held fully resident (`this.kgKUs`, `this.kgEdges`, :60-61), a multi-GB heap.

**Canonical-term boost: O(1,722) substring tests per query plus O(chunks x matched terms).** The 1,722-entry list includes 101 case-duplicate groups (measured), i.e. ~6% pure waste, and terms as generic as 'care','soul','time','form','being','world'. At 100x ontology size this is a full scan of ~170,000 strings per query with `String.includes` — and its precision collapses long before its performance does.

**Cache: 1,000 entries, O(n) eviction, no corpus coupling.** :1442-1456 walks all 1,000 entries per insert at capacity; each entry holds up to 28 full chunk bodies (~84 MB at 3 KB/chunk); nothing invalidates on re-ingest.

**Span generation: unbounded.** faceted-retrieval.ts:254 emits a QuoteSpan with a randomUUID and three SHA-256 hashes for every sentence >= 20 chars in every retrieved chunk — the relevance filter (`isRelevantToFacet`, :343) exists but is never called. 15 chunks/facet x ~10-60 sentences = 150-900 spans/facet, x 3 hashes.
architecture_assessment.claim_level_readiness:
Carrying claim-level and clause-level records at ~100x volume requires four things this code does not have, in dependency order.

**1. Stable, addressable identity for every retrieved unit.** Today the pipeline reaches for `metadata.chunk_id` and `metadata.source_id`, neither of which exists, at 20 sites. The unique id is already computed at ingest (`{doc_id}:{idx:05d}`, run_ingest_phase2.py:659/:699) and already lands on `chunk.chunkId` at smart-retrieval-layer.ts:973 — it is simply never used. Claim-level records need a strictly finer id (`{doc_id}:{chunk_idx}:{clause_span}`) and the current code cannot even carry the coarse one correctly. This is a prerequisite, not an enhancement, and it is a ~20-line fix.

**2. Immutable source text.** Claim and clause records are offsets into a document. Every offset in the system today is an offset into a mutable, in-place-rewritten `chunk.content` (retrieval-stage.ts:319, :346), and the rewrite is not even a truncation — it is a re-ordering-preserving collage (retrieval-utils.ts:352-370). Until retrieval output is immutable and the trimmed display form is a separate field, no offset-based record can be trusted. Same fix scope: a `sourceText`/`clean_text` field on ContextChunk plus removing three mutation sites.

**3. An index that can address the corpus.** compiled-index.json currently stores concept names and free-text `units` labels. To drive claim-level retrieval it must store, per claim: the doc_id, the character span, the ontology nodes it instantiates, the edges it participates in, and a vector. That is a schema change in the compiler and a new storage layer — 17,736 edges and 357 unit records reportedly reach runtime today as ZERO, and the reason is that nothing in the retrieval path can consume a record that lacks a chunk address.

**4. Indexed lookup instead of linear scan.** Every graph operation in the retrieval layer is a `for...of` over the full array. At claim-level granularity the KU set becomes the claim set — the very thing that grows 100x — and `for (const ku of kus)` inside `chunks.map(...)` (smart-retrieval-layer.ts:586-596) becomes the dominant cost. Required: a term-to-claim inverted index and a concept-to-edge adjacency map, built once per index generation and persisted (SQLite or the existing AgentDB), so boosting is O(terms in chunk) lookups rather than O(total claims).

One more thing that must change and is easy to miss: **there is no way to tell a successful run from a totally ungrounded one.** Seven of eight failure paths in retrieval-stage use `recordWarning`, which `computePipelineHealth` (stage-types.ts:63-67) does not consult; two swallow silently; and semanticSearch returns `[]` on every infrastructure error rather than throwing, so the documented F-13 circuit breaker at :306-313 never fires. An index of a million claims that cannot report when it retrieved zero of them is not a foundation for anything.
architecture_assessment.harden_or_replace:
**Harden the retrieval layer. Replace the scoring stack and the graph-boost layer. Rebuild the index schema.** That split is the honest answer, and here is the evidence for each part.

**Harden — the plumbing is sound and the defects are small and local.** The HTTP wiring to the embedding API and Chroma (:898-945) is correct. The query-embedding asymmetry fix (`kind: 'query'` at :901) is right and was hard-won. The rerank integration (:1220-1286) is well-structured: AbortController timeout, index validation, `retrievalScore` preserved for observability, safe degradation. The Zod validation at the JSONL boundary (types.ts:93-134) is genuinely good. The mtime-invalidating shared index loader (jsonl-loaders.ts:198-218) is the right pattern — it is just bypassed by two other caches. Crucially, my six CRITICAL findings are **all small**: the de-dup key is ~20 one-line edits; cache aliasing is ~6 lines; the collage is ~15; `collections` as a metadata `$in` filter is ~10 (the ingest already writes `collection` into chunk metadata at run_ingest_phase2.py:1742); the hybridSearch 4th parameter is ~15; empty-result caching and the latched `collectionResolved` are ~12. Call it 200-300 lines to eliminate every CRITICAL and most HIGH findings. A rewrite would cost 10x that and would re-derive the same HTTP layer.

**Replace the scoring stack — it is not tunable, it is incoherent.** Three score scales are mixed with no normalisation: cosine in [0,1], cross-encoder scores on the reranker's own scale, and a fabricated constant 0.85 (retrieval-stage.ts:305). Two clamped boosts run *after* the reranker and saturate its output at 1.0. `minRelevance` means cosine in one branch of mergeResults and a 0.7-weighted composite in the other (:1313-1327). The 0.6 threshold in faceted-retrieval means something different depending on whether keyword search happened to return anything. You cannot tune your way out of this; the ordering of the stages is wrong. Replacement is small in code (~100 lines: one score-fusion function, priors applied to `retrievalScore`, reranker last, weights on an eval set) but it is a redesign, not a patch. The existing eval harness (scripts/test-rerank-wiring.ts) is the right place to validate it.

**Replace the graph-boost layer outright.** smart-retrieval-layer.ts:565-707 is three nested linear scans, an unbounded in-memory graph, and substring `includes` matching standing in for semantics (:648, :684). Nothing about it survives 100x. The 200-300-line inverted-index rewrite described above is the replacement.

**Rebuild the index schema — this is the real project.** The index cannot carry claim-level records because it stores no addresses. That is not a bug in this scope's files; it is the compiler's output shape. Until compiled-index.json emits per-claim `{doc_id, span, concepts, edges, vector}`, the retrieval layer has nothing to be index-first *about*.

**Is index-first ordering implementable here, and what does it cost?** Implementable, yes — but not as a reordering of existing calls, because the two stores are not commensurable. Chroma indexes chunk vectors; the compiled index holds concept names with no chunk addresses. "Index first, Chroma fallback" today would mean "look up a concept name, get back a definition string and a list of unit labels, and then have no way to turn any of it into a chunk." Making it real needs, in order: (1) the compiler emits chunk-addressed records (schema change, ~1-2 weeks); (2) those records get their own vector store or a second Chroma collection (~1 week, and the `collections` plumbing from finding 4 is a prerequisite because today only one collection is reachable); (3) retrieveContext gains a two-stage path — resolve query concepts against the index, fetch index-addressed chunks directly, then use Chroma only to fill the remainder (~150 lines); (4) score fusion across the two sources (the redesign above). Roughly 4-6 weeks, and steps 1 and 2 are outside this scope's files. The dependency worth stating plainly: **do not build index-first retrieval on top of a de-duplication key that collapses the corpus by page number.** Fix identity first — it is the cheapest change in this entire report and everything else stands on it.

findings.claim: The bold-field regex requires at least one space after the dash (`-\s+\*\*`). A line written `-**Definition**: ...` falls to the plain-dash arm, producing field key '**definition**' — so the definition is stored under a key nothing reads and the node ships with an empty definition.

findings.fix_sketch: Apply strip_bold to the key produced by the plain-dash arm and record a defect for any field key outside the known schema. ~5 lines.

findings.claim: The plain-dash arm turns any line beginning with '-' containing a colon within its first 40 characters into a named field, so ordinary prose bullets silently become node metadata; and if the colon is the first surviving character the key is empty and the value is dropped.
findings.failure_scenario: A definition continued as `- Note: this qualification matters` becomes a field named 'note' and terminates the previous field. A line `---: stray` has lstrip("- ") strip the dashes leaving ': stray'; split(':',1) gives ['', ' stray'], so current_key = '' — the value is never stored (guarded by `if current_key` at :706 and :723) and the accumulator is left in a falsy state, after which continuation lines are dropped entirely.
findings.consequence: Free-text bullets become schema keys; the empty-key path is a silent hole. Seven non-schema keys already occur in the live parse ('node a','node b','dependency edge','conflict edge','synthesis','dependency','conflict'), all discarded at :756-767.
findings.fix_sketch: Restrict the plain-dash arm to a closed set of known field names; treat anything else as continuation text. ~8 lines.

findings.failure_scenario: The authoring pipeline already emits contributors and cross_pipeline_links per node plus a structured contested_concepts list. At 100x volume the artifact is ~66 MB of JSON loaded and parsed in full into a module-level cache with no invalidation; at claim/clause granularity it is orders of magnitude beyond that.

prior_claim_verdicts.correction: Three corrections.
