architecture_assessment.ceiling:
Three independent ceilings, all reachable well before 100x.

(1) SCORING — corpus-index-provider.ts:112-118 is O(nodes x topicTerms) with a fresh RegExp compiled per (term, node) pair at :86 plus a string join per node at :113-116. A 27-term topic against today's 701 nodes = ~18,927 RegExp constructions and 701 joins PER CALL. At 100x (70,100 nodes) that is ~1.9M RegExp constructions per call, and the rolling-context path calls it once per section. There is no inverted index, no precomputed searchText, no early termination.

(2) MEMORY — jsonl-loaders.ts:210-211 does readFileSync + JSON.parse of the whole file and holds the object graph for the process lifetime. Today 531,408 bytes. At 100x: ~53MB of JSON parsed into a JS object graph, roughly 200-400MB resident. Add claim-level records and the file is 10-50x larger again (0.5-2.5GB) — not loadable this way at all.

(3) PROMPT — the hard cap is not tokens, it is the fixed slice() constants. Measured on a representative on-topic run: ontologyLines 2,977 chars, hookLines 800, tensionLines 2,915 = 6,692 chars, which is 1.26% of compiled-index.json's 531,408 bytes. The caps are 12 nodes / 3 hooks / 5 tensions with definitions cut at 200 chars, bridges at 150, descriptions at 200, units at 5. At 100x volume those constants do not move, so the ABSOLUTE index content reaching the model stays at ~6,700 chars while the fraction falls to 0.0126%. The system does not degrade at scale — it stays exactly as thin while the index behind it grows 100x. That is the more damaging failure mode, because nothing looks broken.

Token headroom for reference: the measured full gold-standard prompt (no chunks) is 15,723 chars / ~3,931 tokens, of which 47.2% is index-derived; with 28 chunks it is ~28,000 chars / ~7,000 tokens against a 1M-token window. There are roughly 140x of unused window. The ceiling is entirely self-imposed by the caps and by estimateTokenBudget's wrong 200,000-token assumption (pipeline-utils.ts:47).
architecture_assessment.harden_or_replace:
HARDEN the pipeline, REPLACE the selector and the transport format.

The case for keeping the pipeline: everything downstream of selection is correct and load-bearing. gold-standard-prompt-builder.ts is a clean pure function with a stable options interface (:28-51), used identically by the CLI pipeline and the dashboard API. The section ordering, the recency-bias final directive (:811-818), the LaTeX/markdown fork (buildSubsectionPrompt), the rolling-context citation tracker (orchestrator:1048-1054, :1191-1201), the shared-pool eviction by author citation count (:1111-1119), and the chunk-to-section term-overlap allocator (:887-950) are real, working, hard-won mechanisms. Throwing them away to fix a scorer would be a large unforced loss. The v2 staged pipeline (retrieval → drafting → validation) with PipelineContext's three-tier hardFailures/degradedEvents/warnings is a sound skeleton. A rewrite is 6-12 months that would reproduce most of this.

The case for replacing two specific components: corpus-index-provider.ts's scoreCandidate (:81-91) cannot be fixed by tuning. No stopword list, no normalization, no floor, ranking by raw substring count — which is why 'supply chain logistics optimization in regional distribution warehouses' retrieves EEG connectivity, gaze variance, and Assemblage with a straight face. Every parameter you could tune is already at its degenerate value. Replace it with an embedding query against the same service chunk retrieval already uses, or at minimum BM25 with a floor: ~150 lines that delete the single largest source of prompt noise.

And the transport format: passing pre-rendered strings (ontologyLines: string[]) instead of structured records is what makes the duplicate-bridge filter impossible to write correctly (the id is not in the string), what makes provenance unattachable, and what makes budget-aware truncation impossible. Change GoldStandardPromptOptions to take OntologyNode[] / CrossPipelineHook[] / TensionEdge[] and render inside the builder — ~120 lines, and it unblocks four other findings at once.

Ordered plan: (1) fix the six CRITICALs — the flag drop, the 'Unknown' bridge, the duplicate injection, the Source Index/truncation mismatch, the sectionConstraints misalignment, the zero-revision gauntlet; (2) replace scoreCandidate; (3) switch to structured records end-to-end; (4) add a units store with per-node expansion; (5) only then consider claim-level. Steps 1-3 are ~400 lines and make the current architecture trustworthy. Step 4 is where the real programme starts.
architecture_assessment.claim_level_readiness:
Six things have to change, in order.

(1) A UNIT STORE. Today unit IDs are injected as opaque tokens (corpus-index-provider.ts:125 `[${node.units.slice(0, 5).join(', ')}]`) with nothing to resolve them against — CompiledIndex has exactly four content keys (:52-58) and 4,059 unit references point at nothing. compiled-index.json must gain a `units` map (id → {text, source, locus, page}) before ANY unit-level injection is possible. One node already carries 973 units, silently cut to 5 — a compiler corruption artifact that would become 973 dangling claim pointers.

(2) STRUCTURED TRANSPORT. GoldStandardPromptOptions takes string[] for ontologyNodes/crossPipelineHooks/tensionEdges (:34-36). Claim-level records need id, text, locus, source, confidence, and support/attack edges — none of which survive pre-rendering. This is also the change that fixes the dead dedup filter and makes provenance attachable.

(3) A REAL SELECTOR. Substring frequency over ≥4-char tokens does not survive the density increase. At 100x with claim-level granularity the candidate set is ~10^6 records; `.map(...).filter(score>0).sort(...).slice(0,12)` over that, per section, is not viable, and the noise floor (an off-topic query already returns 12 nodes today) becomes total. Needs an embedding or BM25 index built at compile time, not scanned at query time.

(4) A TOKEN BUDGET THAT MEASURES THE PROMPT. estimateTokenBudget (pipeline-utils.ts:33-58) excludes every index block, the topic, the boilerplate, and the rolling context; assumes a 200,000-token window against 1M-token models; and its suggestedMaxOutput is discarded at the call site (orchestrator:3579-3582). At claim level the index block becomes the DOMINANT prompt component, so budget allocation has to be real and has to trim by relevance rather than by a slice() constant.

(5) STREAMING / INDEXED LOAD. readFileSync + JSON.parse of the whole file (jsonl-loaders.ts:210-211) does not survive a claim-level index. Needs SQLite or a memory-mapped columnar store with mtime-scoped invalidation — and the invalidation must reset derived state, which today it does not (_hooksDerivationDone, cross-author-utils.ts:56).

(6) VALIDATION AT LOAD. The current index already ships records that produce nonsense prompts: 31 hooks with empty targetConcept, a hook whose sourceConcept is the literal heading 'Specific hooks', a targetConcept carrying an inline '[INTERP-high]' tag, bridge bodies beginning with markdown bullets. At claim level these become fabricated claims presented as verified. A schema validator that rejects and LOGS bad records is a precondition, not a nicety.

Token arithmetic for the target state: at ~4 chars/token a 1M-token window is ~4M chars. Reserving 128K tokens for output and ~40K for chunks/style/boilerplate leaves roughly 800K tokens = ~3.2M chars for index content. At ~300 chars per claim record with locus and provenance that is ~10,000 claim records per prompt, against today's 6,692 chars / ~19 records. The window is not the constraint. Selection quality is — injecting 10,000 claims chosen by substring frequency would be strictly worse than injecting 19.
architecture_assessment.current_capability:
The drafting LLM sees exactly five index-derived blocks, all built from three pre-rendered string arrays produced by corpus-index-provider.ts:120-157 and threaded through write-pipeline-orchestrator.ts:2115-2131 (legacy) / stages/retrieval-stage.ts:468-483 (v2) into gold-standard-prompt-builder.ts.

LITERAL BLOCKS AND CAPS (v2, whitelist/use-corpus path):
- `## CANONICAL CONCEPT NODES (from corpus ontology)` + "These are the established canonical names and definitions for key concepts in the corpus. Use canonical forms and Greek/German terms consistently. Prefer these definitions over paraphrase." (builder:690-693). Cap 12 nodes (retrieval-stage:471). Line format `- **{greek||name}**{ (translit)}{: definition[0:200]}{ [unit1..unit5]}` (provider:120-127).
- `## MANDATORY THEORETICAL SYNTHESIS` + "You MUST integrate this connection into your argument — it is a verified, high-confidence interpretive link" (builder:708-711). Cap 1 (cross-author-utils:498).
- `## CROSS-PIPELINE INTERPRETIVE HOOKS` + "These are high-confidence [INTERP-high] connections verified against primary sources." (builder:731-733). Cap 3 (retrieval-stage:472). Format `- HOOK [srcText → tgtText]: srcConcept ↔ tgtConcept — bridge[0:150] [tag]` (provider:137-144).
- `## CONCEPTUAL TENSIONS (from corpus analysis)` + "Acknowledge and engage them — do not paper over them" (builder:742-745). Cap 5 (retrieval-stage:473). Format `- TENSION [id]: nodeA ↔ nodeB — description[0:200] [units]` (provider:152-157).
- `## STRUCTURAL RELATIONSHIPS (from reasoning graph)` (builder:673-683) — sourced from god-reason/reasoning.jsonl, not compiled-index.json. Cap 30 (retrieval-stage:458).

ORDERING: role framing → style profile → Lanham → writing task → critical constraints → corpus chunks → knowledge units → structural relationships → CANONICAL CONCEPT NODES → MANDATORY THEORETICAL SYNTHESIS → CROSS-PIPELINE HOOKS → CONCEPTUAL TENSIONS → output format → final directive. The index blocks sit AFTER the chunks and BEFORE the output-format block.

MEASURED SIZES (reproduced with the real modules on a representative on-topic dissertation prompt): ontologyLines 2,977 chars (~745 tok), hookLines 800 chars (~200 tok), tensionLines 2,915 chars (~729 tok). Full gold-standard prompt with index blocks and zero chunks: 15,723 chars (~3,931 tok); without them 8,297 chars (~2,075 tok) — index-derived content is 47.2% of the prompt. Injected index bytes are 6,692 of 531,408 = 1.26% of the index reaches the model.

FIELD BY FIELD, WHAT REACHES THE MODEL: node.greek||name, node.transliteration, node.definition[0:200], node.units[0:5] as bare IDs. NOT injected: node.text (the source work — so concept nodes are unattributable), node.type, node.translation, node.centralityTier. Tensions: id, nodeA, nodeB, description[0:200], units. NOT injected: dependencyRelation, conflictRelation (the actual structure of the tension), text (source). Hooks: sourceText, targetText, sourceConcept, targetConcept, bridge[0:150], tag. NOT injected: relevance, title. canonicalTerms (1,722 entries) NEVER reach any prompt — used only for retrieval boosting (smart-retrieval-layer.ts:265) and stopword protection (:198-215).

So the accurate statement is stronger than 'concept names': the prompt carries concept names, 200-char definition prefixes with no source attribution, and dangling unit-ID pointers into a store that does not exist at runtime.

findings.claim: run_ingest.py writes manifest records with status="ok" and a chunk count while producing ZERO embeddings and ZERO Chroma writes. 531 of the 696 latest manifest records (76%) are of exactly this shape, and every one of them has no vectors in the store.
findings.evidence: run_ingest.py docstring :13 `- NO embeddings`. record_base at :395-408 = `{"path_abs","path_rel","collection","mtime","sha256","doc_id","status","chunks","error","ts","meta"}` — no `phase`, no `fidelity_mode`, no store reference. :445-447 `record_base["chunks"] = len(chunks)` / `record_base["status"] = "ok"` / `record_base["error"] = None`; :460 `append_manifest(manifest_path, record_base)`. MEASURED: latest-record key-set of a phase-less record is byte-for-byte that list; 531 latest records lack the `phase` key entirely; their doc_ids intersected against the 163 distinct doc_ids in chroma.sqlite3 segment f4724ac2 give `doc_id PRESENT in chroma: 163 / ABSENT: 531 / chunks claimed by ABSENT docs: 3249 / phase dist of ABSENT: Counter({None: 531})`.
findings.failure_scenario: `python3 scripts/ingest/run_ingest.py --root corpus` is run (watch_corpus.py:134-140 does this on every file event). It hashes, chunks, prints a plan, and appends `{"status":"ok","chunks":37,...}`. Nothing is embedded. Any consumer that treats manifest.jsonl as the record of what is retrievable — audit_ingest, verify_ingest, god_learn, or a human — reads 694 ok documents and 15,107 chunks. The store holds 163 documents and 11,858 chunks.
findings.consequence: The system's own record of what has been ingested is wrong about 76% of its rows. 3,249 chunks are asserted as ingested and do not exist. 516 .md + 15 .txt documents — including 518 under corpus/index/ — are invisible to retrieval while being reported as complete.
findings.fix_sketch: `status` must not be a single flat token shared by a planner and a writer. Add a required `stage` discriminator written by whoever actually committed vectors (`"planned"` from run_ingest.py, `"stored"` only after coll.upsert returns), and make every reader require `stage=="stored"`. ~30 lines across run_ingest.py, run_ingest_phase2.py, audit_ingest.py, verify_ingest.py. The 531 existing rows must be rewritten or the manifest re-derived from Chroma.

findings.claim: run_ingest.py's skip predicate checks only sha256+status and ignores `phase` entirely, so the 531 phase-less no-vector records are permanently self-perpetuating: re-running Phase 1 skips them forever and never upgrades them.
findings.evidence:
```
167 def should_skip(path_abs: Path, sha256_hex: str, latest_manifest: Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]]) -> bool:
168     rec = latest_manifest.get(str(path_abs))
169     if not rec:
170         return False
171     return (rec.get("sha256") == sha256_hex) and (rec.get("status") == "ok")
```
Compare run_ingest_phase2.py:324 which does check phase: `phase_ok = int(rec.get("phase") or 0) >= 2`.
findings.failure_scenario: A corpus .md file is ingested once by run_ingest.py → record `{status:ok, chunks:12, no phase}`. Every subsequent run_ingest.py invocation hits :171, returns True, `continue`s at :420 without appending anything. The record is never superseded. Only run_ingest_phase2.py can rescue it, and watch_corpus.py:147-153 runs it over the whole root — but if that phase-2 run fails for ANY file it returns 1 (:1896) and watch_corpus logs `Phase 2 failed` at :156 and returns, leaving the record phase-less.
findings.consequence: A permanently stuck no-vector state that no re-run of the Phase-1 tool can clear. This is the exact mechanism that produced the 518 stuck corpus/index/ records.
findings.fix_sketch: Make should_skip require the same `stage=="stored"` discriminator, or delete run_ingest.py entirely (it is a superseded skeleton whose only remaining effect is corrupting the manifest). Deletion is ~1 line in watch_corpus.py:133-144 plus removing the file.

findings.claim: parallel_ingest.py catches and logs the ChromaDB upsert exception, then _flush_batch unconditionally reports the whole batch as written. A store that rejects every write yields "64 chunks written", a clean summary, and exit code 0.
findings.evidence:
```
589     try:
590         coll.upsert(ids=ids, documents=documents, embeddings=embeddings, metadatas=metadatas)
591     except Exception as e:
592         logger.error(f"ChromaDB upsert failed: {e}")
```
_write_to_db returns None. The caller:
```
659     try:
660         vecs = embed_texts(texts, session)
661         _write_to_db(batch, vecs, coll, manifest_path)
662         return len(batch), 0
```
`return len(batch), 0` is reached whether or not the upsert threw. That value becomes `total_written` (:613, :635) and is printed at :644 and :873. main() returns `0 if failed == 0 else 1` at :906 — `failed` counts producer results only, never write failures.
findings.failure_scenario: Chroma is up enough for `get_or_create_collection` at :601 but rejects upserts (dimension mismatch after an embedder swap, disk full, metadata value too large, HTTP 413 on a large `raw_content`). Every batch logs one ERROR line into a stderr stream nobody reads. Summary prints `Chunks written: 11858`, `Chunks dropped: 0`, exit 0. Then :832-845 appends manifest records with `"status": "ok", "phase": 2, "chunks": N`.
findings.consequence: A complete ingestion run can write nothing at all and report total success, and then poison the manifest with phase-2 ok records that block future re-ingestion (should_skip_phase2 :324 accepts phase>=2). Worse than the run_ingest.py case because these records DO carry a passing phase.
findings.fix_sketch: _write_to_db must return a bool/raise; _flush_batch must return `(0, len(batch))` on write failure and the run must exit non-zero. ~10 lines. Additionally the manifest write at :832 must be conditioned on the consumer's actual written set, not on producer results.

findings.claim: parallel_ingest.py's skip check compares the first 12 hex chars of a first-64KB hash against the first 12 hex chars of a stored FULL-file hash. For any file larger than 64 KB these are different hash functions and can never agree, so the skip path is dead and every PDF over 64 KB is re-extracted and re-embedded on every run.
findings.evidence:
```
187         sha = hashlib.sha256(pdf_path.read_bytes()[:65536]).hexdigest()[:12]
188         full_sha = hashlib.sha256(pdf_path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()
...
196         if prev and prev.get("status") == "ok" and prev.get("sha256", "")[:12] == sha and not force:
```
The manifest stores `full_sha` (:313 `sha256=full_sha`, :837 `hashlib.sha256(...read_bytes()).hexdigest()`). run_ingest_phase2.py:1044-1046 documents this exact bug as already fixed there: "Compare the FULL-file sha (the manifest stores the full sha; the old first-64KB sha never matched for files >64KB, so every done doc was wastefully re-fetched)." The fix was never ported to parallel_ingest.py.
findings.failure_scenario: Any of the 292 corpus PDFs (all >64 KB) is re-run through parallel_ingest.py. :196 is False. Marker GPU extraction, PyMuPDF extraction, fidelity gate, chunking, and embedding all re-execute. On a 292-PDF / 3 GB corpus that is hours of GPU time per invocation with no work skipped.
findings.consequence: The incremental-ingest contract does not exist on this code path. At 100x volume this makes parallel_ingest.py unusable — every run is a full re-ingest. It also means every run re-mints identical chunk ids and re-upserts, masking the problem as "idempotent" rather than "never skipping".
findings.fix_sketch: `if prev and prev.get("status")=="ok" and prev.get("sha256")==full_sha and not force`. Delete the 64KB `sha` variable and the duplicated `read_bytes()`. 3 lines.

summary:
I read all six scoped files end to end plus the manifest and the live Chroma store, and the headline is not a code defect — it is a measured, currently-live divergence between what the system says it has ingested and what it actually holds.

MEASURED: manifest.jsonl holds 1,182 records, 696 distinct path_abs, 694 with status="ok" claiming 15,107 chunks. The live knowledge_chunks collection holds 11,858 rows across 163 distinct doc_ids. Intersecting doc_ids: 163 present, **531 absent, claiming 3,249 chunks that do not exist**. The correlation is perfect and diagnostic — all 531 absent records have `phase: None` (the key is missing entirely), and that key-set is byte-for-byte run_ingest.py's `record_base` at :395-408. run_ingest.py's own docstring says `- NO embeddings` (:13). It writes `status: "ok"` and a chunk count for work it never did (:445-447, :460), and its skip predicate at :167-171 ignores `phase`, so those records are permanently self-perpetuating. 518 of them are under corpus/index/, matching the prior claim of 518/522 exactly. A further 132 PDFs / 868.6 MB — the entire `boredom` (50) and `pedagogy` (35) clusters — have no manifest record at all, which makes audit_ingest exit 1 and abort god_learn's substrate pipeline via tee_run's CalledProcessError.

All four scoped prior claims land. SKIP_DIRS is verbatim identical at :978/:365/:69 with "index" absent — and a SKIP_DIRS-applied walk finds 908 of 1,212 files (75%) under corpus/index/, 13.8 MB of the compiler's own source markdown, which god_learn.py:338 invokes the ingester over WITHOUT --pdf-only. should_skip_phase2:324 is verbatim. doc_id/chunk-id derivation is verbatim, but there are six minting sites across three files, not three, and the namespace breaks on a mere `--root` change, not only a file move. The delete claim is PARTIAL: :1830 is right, its feeding `coll.get` is at :1687 not :1686, and there is a **second** delete at reingest_layout.py:173 that is keyed on doc_id instead of path_rel and uses delete-then-upsert — the inverse of the safety ordering run_ingest_phase2.py:1681-1685 documents. No purge script exists; I found 13 already-orphaned chunks for a deleted file that nothing in the repo can reach.

Beyond the prior claims, the most serious new findings are: parallel_ingest.py:589-592 swallows the ChromaDB upsert exception and :662 reports the batch as written anyway, so a run that stores nothing exits 0 with a clean summary; its skip check at :196 compares a 64KB-prefix hash against a full-file hash and therefore never fires for any file over 64 KB; and its bbox attachment at :348-352 is the positional lookup that run_ingest_phase2.py:1694-1697 documents as a fixed bug — Marker's boxes land on the wrong chunks. In run_ingest_phase2.py, `--require-full` is a no-op unless `--marker` is also passed (:1021 sits inside the `if MARKER_ENABLED:` arm), so the flag that exists to prevent a degraded overwrite silently permits one.

Two hard ceilings. `marker_cache` (:1030) holds every PDF's full Marker JSON for the whole run with no eviction — it pre-fetches ALL before processing ANY. And `raw_content` (:1757) stores every chunk's pre-clean text a second time as Chroma metadata: MEASURED 38.4 MB against 46.6 MB of documents, 106.6 MB of metadata total, ~9 KB per chunk.

On the user's goal: the .md path — 880 of 1,212 corpus files — produces chunks with page_start/page_end hard-coded to None (:700). I verified in the store that all 27 .md chunks have zero page_start and zero bboxes rows. The majority file format carries no positional anchor at all.

architecture_assessment.current_capability:
This code does one thing competently: it walks a directory, turns PDFs into ~1000-token prose chunks with page-level and (on the Marker path) bbox-level provenance, embeds them at 1536-D, and upserts them into a single flat Chroma collection. The Marker/PyMuPDF/pdftotext tiering with a scholarly fidelity gate is genuinely good work — run_ingest_phase2.py:1236-1277 routes text and bboxes independently, and the upsert-then-delete ordering at :1681-1831 is a correct and deliberate data-safety design.

That is the whole capability. Concretely, the unit of record is a chunk: 42 flat scalar metadata keys, three of which (`bboxes`, `locators`, `raw_content`) are JSON strings Chroma cannot filter on. There is no claim, no clause, no sentence, no assertion, no relation. The finest addressable granularity is `{doc_id}:{idx:05d}` — an 800-1200 token blob. The closest thing to a sub-chunk record is `extract_locators_with_bbox` (markdown_chunker.py:307-331), which finds Bekker/Stephanus strings by regex and attaches them by naked substring containment (run_ingest_phase2.py:1794) — 1,947 of 11,858 chunks carry one.

And the capability is not currently being exercised over the corpus it is pointed at. MEASURED: 163 of 694 manifest-"ok" documents actually have vectors. 132 PDFs (868.6 MB) have never been ingested. 998 corpus files (525 .json, 279 .csv, 68 .mmd, 22 .vtt) are outside ALLOWED_EXTS entirely. The .md path — 880 of 1,212 walkable files — produces chunks with no page, no bbox, and no locator.
architecture_assessment.ceiling:
Three hard numbers, in the order they will be hit.

1. **marker_cache OOM, at roughly 1,500-3,000 PDFs.** run_ingest_phase2.py:1030 allocates one dict and :1069-1081 fills it with every PDF's complete Marker JSON block tree before the main loop at :1084 consumes the first entry. Nothing evicts (grep for `marker_cache` returns four lines: :1030 declare, :1076 write, :1081 log, :1204 read). A Marker tree for a 400-page book is a nested structure with per-block html, bbox, polygon and children for every text line — tens of MB. At today's 292 PDFs this is already gigabytes on a box that concurrently runs Marker and a ~7-8 GB embedding model on the same GPU. At 29,200 PDFs it is not close.

2. **Metadata storage, at roughly 1.2M chunks.** MEASURED over vector_db_1536/chroma.sqlite3 segment f4724ac2: 11,858 chunks carry 106,596,237 bytes of metadata string — ~9 KB per chunk — of which `raw_content` alone is 38,451,116 bytes (an 82% duplicate of the 46,640,025 bytes of documents) and `bboxes` is 13,789,791. The file is already 3,143,405,568 bytes. Linear extrapolation to 100x: ~10.7 GB of sqlite metadata before the HNSW index. Every `coll.get(where={'path_rel': ...})` at :1687 — once per document per run — queries that table.

3. **Incremental cost, immediately.** run_ingest_phase2.py hashes every PDF twice per run (:1048 in the pre-fetch filter, :1136 in the main loop). parallel_ingest.py reads each file's full bytes at :187, again at :188, again at :837, and a fourth time at :838. watch_corpus.py:134-153 ignores the changed path entirely and re-walks the whole root twice per file event. So the cost of ingesting one new document is already O(corpus_bytes), not O(document_bytes). At 100x, a single save under watch mode would take longer than the 5-second debounce window and events would accumulate unboundedly in `self.pending` (:98).

A fourth, softer ceiling: verify_ingest.py:122 pulls every embedding for a document over HTTP to inspect three (`include=["embeddings"]` with `to_check = min(sample_n, len(embs))` at :138), so verification time scales with total vector volume rather than document count — and verification is what gates god_learn's substrate pipeline at god_learn.py:721.
architecture_assessment.claim_level_readiness:
Carrying claim-level and clause-level records at 100x requires four things this code does not have, in dependency order.

**(1) A sub-chunk addressing scheme.** Chunk ids are `{doc_id}:{idx:05d}` where idx is a position in a greedy token-packing pass (:646-681, :684-714). The index is not stable: re-chunking with different token targets, a different extractor winning the fidelity gate, or Marker's `_merge_small_chunks` behaving differently renumbers everything. A claim record pointing at `{doc_id}:00042` is pointing at whatever happened to land in slot 42 that run. Claims need content-addressed ids (hash of the claim span text + source hash) plus a stable character range into the source, so that re-extraction can be diffed rather than renumbered. Today no character offsets are computed anywhere — `clean_corpus_text` (:546-633) rewrites the text through four transformation stages (locator-line deletion, dehyphenation, line joining, whitespace collapse) with no offset map, so even the mapping from cleaned text back to the raw file is unrecoverable. That offset map is the prerequisite for everything else.

**(2) A store that can hold relations.** Chroma metadata accepts only str/int/float/bool/None — run_ingest_phase2.py:1804-1808 enforces this by `str()`-ing anything else, which is why `bboxes` and `locators` are JSON strings. A JSON string is invisible to `where`. So "find every claim that contradicts claim X" is not a query; it is a full collection scan plus client-side JSON parsing. 100x makes that impossible. Claims and clauses need a relational store (sqlite/postgres) holding typed rows — claim(id, doc_id, char_start, char_end, page, bbox, text, kind), clause(claim_id, ...), edge(claim_a, claim_b, relation, strength, evidence) — with Chroma used only as the vector index over claim text, joined by id. That is the single most consequential structural change.

**(3) A walk that admits structured formats.** The 998 non-ALLOWED_EXTS files under corpus/ — 525 .json, 279 .csv — are exactly the edge/unit/tension records that constitute "every point of connection." Prose chunking cannot ingest them; they need typed loaders writing typed rows. That lane does not exist. Note the inverse problem too: 908 index/ files that are structural source ARE walkable and get prose-chunked, so the pipeline has the polarity backwards in both directions.

**(4) A manifest that cannot lie.** At 100x, hand-reconciliation is impossible, so the manifest must be trustworthy by construction. Today it is a plain append-only JSONL with no schema validation (`load_latest_manifest_by_path` at :293-309 silently `continue`s past unparseable lines and validates nothing on the ones that parse), written by three different producers with three different schemas (run_ingest.py's 11 keys with no phase; parallel_ingest.py's 12 keys with phase 2; run_ingest_phase2.py's 32 keys with phase 5), rewritten in place by god_learn.py:700-701, and — the measured consequence — wrong about 531 of 696 rows.

Rough magnitude for a claim/clause layer built on a corrected foundation: character-offset plumbing through cleaning and chunking ~200 lines; a relational claim/clause/edge schema plus writers ~400; typed loaders for .csv/.json ~250; extraction of claims from chunk text (the actual NLP/LLM work) is the bulk and is not a line-count question.
architecture_assessment.harden_or_replace:
**Harden the extraction spine. Replace the record layer and the walk. Delete run_ingest.py.**

The case for hardening the spine is that the expensive, hard-won part is correct. run_ingest_phase2.py:1236-1277 gets a genuinely subtle thing right — it separates "who wins for prose text" from "who provides bboxes and tables," so a document can take pdftotext's more faithful prose while keeping Marker's visual provenance (:1258-1264). The upsert-then-delete ordering at :1681-1831 is deliberate, commented, and correct. The Marker pool resolution (:147-163) returns all reachable servers specifically so a half-down WRAITH cannot poison the round-robin. The adaptive embedding batch splitter (:775-820) is real engineering. None of that should be thrown away, and none of it is what is broken.

The case for replacing the record layer is the measurement. 531 of 696 manifest rows are wrong; the store's finest granularity is a 1000-token blob; the three richest fields are JSON strings the query engine cannot see; and the only reconciliation key in the tree is exact path_rel string equality, which has already produced 13 unreachable orphans. That is not a hardening problem. A `stage` discriminator would fix the 531 rows, but it would not make a chunk into a claim, and it would not let you ask a relational question.

The case for deleting run_ingest.py outright is that it is a superseded Phase-1 skeleton whose sole remaining effect on the system is to corrupt the manifest — 531 no-vector "ok" records, permanently sticky because its skip predicate at :167-171 ignores phase. It is invoked by exactly one live caller (watch_corpus.py:134-140) and referenced by one broken instruction (missing-source-acquisition.ts:378, which passes a `--input` flag the script does not accept). Removing it is a net subtraction of ~480 lines and removes an entire class of manifest corruption.

The case for replacing the walk is that a deny-list of five dot-directories is the wrong shape for a tree in which 75% of the walkable files are the index's own source. It has to enumerate every non-corpus directory that will ever exist, and it has already failed to enumerate the biggest one. An allow-list of configured collection roots inverts the default from "swept up unless excluded" to "opt-in."

Sequencing, cheapest-first, with the numbers that justify each:

1. Delete run_ingest.py; point watch_corpus.py at run_ingest_phase2.py with a new `--file` argument (~8 lines at :980-986). Fixes 531 bad rows at the source and the O(corpus) per-event cost together.
2. Add "index" to the three SKIP_DIRS sets, or better an allow-list (3-20 lines). Prevents 908 files / 13.8 MB of compiler source from entering retrieval the next time god_learn.py:338 runs.
3. Hoist the `--require-full` check out of the `if MARKER_ENABLED:` arm (2 lines at :1026). Stops a degraded run from overwriting FULL records.
4. Make parallel_ingest.py's _write_to_db raise or return a status (~10 lines at :589-592, :659-662), and fix its skip hash (3 lines at :187-196). Without these two the second ingester cannot be trusted at all.
5. Move `raw_content` to a content-addressed sidecar keyed on the already-computed `raw_sha256` (~10 lines + migration). Recovers 38.4 MB now, ~3.8 GB at 100x.
6. Bound marker_cache — `del marker_cache[path_str]` after :1206 as a two-line stopgap, then the streaming rewrite (~60 lines). This is the wall that decides whether 100x is reachable at all.
7. Write the missing purge_orphans.py (~60 lines). It does not exist and there is no other way to reach the orphans.
8. Then, and only then, build the claim/clause layer on the relational schema — with character offsets threaded through clean_corpus_text and the chunkers as the prerequisite (~200 lines) before any claim extraction is attempted.

Steps 1-7 total roughly 200 lines of change against a 4,000-line tree. The extraction spine survives all of them intact. That ratio is the argument: this is a foundation with a bad record layer bolted on, not an obstacle.

def edge_id(source: str, relation: str, target: str, pipeline: str) -> str:
    """Deterministic edge id (matches god-reason convention: edge_ + 12 hex)."""

    digest = hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
    return f"edge_{digest}"

findings.consequence: Non-unique identifiers in the very layer intended to be the canonical edge store.

architecture_assessment.current_capability:
Across my four files the pipeline can do exactly three things today, and one of them is broken.

(1) normalize-edges.py can column-alias six specific CSVs into an 8-field canonical row: 792 edges from 20,610 available index rows (3.8%). It preserves source/relation/target/domain/units/note and destroys every locator (locus in 110 of 240 files, book_page, page_anchor, provenance, contributor, centrality_tier, evidence_bekker_or_page). It does not normalize relations — 633 distinct values pass through verbatim. It fabricates confidence='medium' where none exists (604 of the 792 output rows).

(2) reason_over_knowledge.py can derive 5,437 similarity edges from 588 knowledge units using char-4-gram Jaccard plus five hardcoded discourse-marker lists. This works and is deterministic — but its output is structurally rejected by the runtime: I validated all 5,437 records against the live zod ReasoningEdgeSchema (src/god-agent/retrieval/types.ts:58-62, source and target both required non-optional) and got PASS 0, DROPPED 5437. The reasoning graph is empty at runtime today.

(3) merge-reasoning-edges.py can anchor those edges to ontology concept names — 83.3% success on a 300-record sample — by scanning each claim against 1,463 terms and taking the first longest match. That is the only code that populates source/target. It writes to the same path Phase 7 truncates, so god-learn update destroys its output; the current file shows this has already happened.

god_learn.py orchestrates all of it and has no failure signal: main() at :751-808 always returns 0, and its one blocking quality gate (:648-661) is provably a no-op on Phase 7 output (I executed check_edge_contradictions on the live file: total_edges 5437, hard 0, soft 0, because :75 requires src && tgt && rel and none exists).

So: the code carries concept names and nothing else into runtime — and at the moment it carries not even those, because the schema mismatch drops 100% of records.
architecture_assessment.ceiling:
Hard numbers, per component.

normalize-edges.py: fixed at 6 files. Not a performance ceiling — a coverage ceiling of 3.8% that does not move with volume. Auto-detection covers 19 of 240 files; the other 221 exit 2. Adding one corpus entry requires editing a literal at :36-41 and a hint tuple at :45-56.

reason_over_knowledge.py: O(n²) pairwise with char_ngrams recomputed inside the inner loop (:297-298, :364-365 — 2 calls per pair, so 345,156 calls for 588 distinct claims). Today: 588 KUs -> 25,334 intra-author + 147,244 cross-author = 172,578 pairs against a max_pairs default of 200,000. That is 86% of budget consumed. One more corpus entry pushes past it, and because the intra-author pass runs first and shares the budget, the cross-author pass at :349 silently stops running with no warning — only a `break`. At 100x (58,800 KUs) total pairs are 1.73 billion, so the cross-author pass would see 0.01% of the space.

merge-reasoning-edges.py: O(records × terms) regex anchoring. Measured 15.9 s for 300 records against 1,463 terms, extrapolating to ~289 s for 5,437. At 100x records with a 10x ontology, ~80 hours single-threaded, with no incremental mode — every run re-anchors everything.

Manifest: 1,087,232 bytes at 1,182 rows, read entirely into memory by deduplicate_manifest (:685) and rewritten non-atomically. At 100x that is ~100 MB read-modify-write with no backup on every `god-learn verify`.

Ingest: 518 of 522 index records carry a falsy phase, so all 516 index markdown files are re-read, re-chunked and re-embedded on every compile. That cost scales linearly with index size — the index gets more expensive to ingest the more index there is.

Edge ids: 48-bit truncation (normalize-edges.py:74). At ~2M edges, ~0.7% birthday collision probability.
architecture_assessment.claim_level_readiness:
Nothing in my scope can carry claim-level or clause-level records, and the obstruction is schema, not scale.

What a claim-level record needs: stable claim id, verbatim claim text, document id, page/Bekker/locus anchor, character offsets into the source, the concept(s) it invokes (plural), the relation(s) it participates in with direction, and provenance for each. Here is what each stage does to that list.

normalize-edges.py collapses it to 8 fields and drops every locator. The 110-file majority header is `source,relation,target,locus,note` and `locus` is read by none of the four resolvers — so the page anchor is discarded for 46% of the index's files. I verified 29 rows across 14 files additionally lose their entire evidential annotation to the `if k is not None` filter at :154 (example: ped-sec-11 line 22, a 200-character CMV-correction rationale, silently dropped).

merge-reasoning-edges.py collapses each claim to ONE concept name — the first-longest ontology term matching anywhere in the text. On a 300-record sample, 26 claims collapsed to 'Perception', 20 to 'οὐσία', 18 to 'Rhetoric'. Two edges anchored to ('Perception','οὐσία') are indistinguishable at runtime even when their claims are unrelated. It also returns on FIRST match, so a claim invoking five concepts records one. And 218 of the 1,463 terms can never match at all because \b fails around their leading/trailing non-word characters — disproportionately the disambiguated terms like 'rhetorical ontology (Gross)' and 'πρὸς ἕν (Focal Meaning)', which are the precise ones.

reason_over_knowledge.py does keep full claim text in evidence[] (:332-335) — the only place in the whole chain where clause-level content survives — but that field is what the runtime schema does not require and the anchoring step discards. Its relation direction is an artifact of ku_id sorting (:319 emits [a.ku_id, b.ku_id] from a bucket sorted at :256) while markers are matched in EITHER claim (:130-146), so roughly half of every asymmetric edge points backwards.

And the raw material is unreachable: ALLOWED_EXTS at run_ingest_phase2.py:197 is {.pdf,.md,.txt}, so the 240 index CSVs holding 20,610 curated edge rows — with their loci, contributors and provenance — have no ingest path at all. 234 of those 240 files have no code path to runtime by any route.

What it would take, concretely: (a) a record schema with claim_id, doc_id, locator, char span, concepts[] and relations[] with direction, replacing the 8-field CSV row and the 5-field reasoning row; (b) a CSV adapter layer covering all 70+ header shapes rather than 6 files; (c) a multi-match, boundary-correct concept matcher (single compiled alternation, not 1,463 sequential regexes); (d) an actual store — sqlite or duckdb — since 2M claim records with spans and multi-valued concepts cannot live in JSONL scanned linearly by three separate uninvalidated in-process caches; (e) direction inference in the relation extractor; (f) exit codes and counters at every stage so that dropping 43% of rows is a build failure rather than silence.
architecture_assessment.harden_or_replace:
Replace normalize-edges.py and merge-reasoning-edges.py. Harden reason_over_knowledge.py and god_learn.py.

The case for replacing normalize-edges.py: its total useful content is a 6-entry path dict, a 10-entry hint list, four ~5-line resolver functions, and an 8-field output schema. Every one of those is wrong for the target. The path dict covers 2.5% of files; the hint list resolves 19 of 240; the resolvers implement first-wins aliasing that provably drops the `works` column on 156 of 156 Aristotle rows; and the 8-field schema has no slot for a locator, which is the field that matters most for a dissertation with Gross-advisor citation rigor. There is no relation normalization to preserve — the function it is named for was never written. Rewriting from the header census (70+ distinct shapes, which I have) is less work than retrofitting, and the retrofit would have to delete every line it kept.

The case for replacing merge-reasoning-edges.py: it has three CRITICAL defects that are all consequences of its shape rather than bugs in it. It reads and writes the same path (:19 == :22) with a truncating open at :206. It is non-idempotent (a second run re-tags manual edges as derivation='phase7'). And its central algorithm — first-longest-term-wins, one concept per claim — is the exact mechanism that reduces the index to concept names. Its inputs are module constants including a dated tmp/ backup directory with no exists() guard. A replacement anchoring service that returns ALL matched concepts with spans, writes to a separate path, and takes argparse arguments shares no code with it.

The case for hardening reason_over_knowledge.py: the pair-generation, bucketing, determinism discipline and stable hashing are sound and worth keeping. Its defects are localized and cheap: hoist char_ngrams out of the inner loop (2 lines, ~600x fewer calls today), give the cross-author pass its own budget and warn on exhaustion (~10 lines), resolve the relative index path from __file__ and log the load (~12 lines), return direction from infer_relation (~20 lines), emit source/target so the runtime schema accepts the output (~30 lines), delete the dead tokenize/term_set/STOPWORDS/TOKEN_RE machinery and the unused `shared` parameter (~25 lines removed). That is roughly a 100-line change to a 507-line file that turns a completely-dropped output into a loadable one.

The case for hardening god_learn.py: the orchestration shape (tee_run streaming with logs, run directories, phase headers) is fine. Three surgical fixes carry most of the value: move deduplicate_manifest out of cmd_verify into an explicit subcommand and stop it deleting status='failed' rows (the single most destructive behaviour I found — 248 index failure records erased by the verify command); make the contradiction gate report how many edges were even eligible so a 0-of-5437 no-op cannot masquerade as a pass; and propagate exit codes so main() can return nonzero. Add 'index' to the three SKIP_DIRS sets, or point --root at a sources subtree, to stop re-embedding 516 index markdown files on every compile.

Overall verdict: the ORCHESTRATION is a foundation. The EDGE NORMALIZATION AND ANCHORING layer is an obstacle — not because it is poorly written but because it implements a lossy 8-field, one-concept-per-claim model that is the opposite of 'every claim and every clause, every point of connection and every weakness.' Keep god_learn.py and reason_over_knowledge.py's skeleton; rewrite the two edge scripts against a claim-level schema and a real store.

Cross-author bridging as a feature does not exist — it is noise injection.

findings.claim: The single bridge selected for injection is, for most topics, hook-de-anima-07 — a record whose targetText, targetConcept, bridge and relevance are ALL empty strings — and the prompt instructs the model that it MUST cite an author literally named 'Unknown'.
findings.evidence:
cross-author-utils.ts:498  `return activeBridges.slice(0, 1);`
gold-standard-prompt-builder.ts:712-716:
  `**Bridge [${bridge.id}]:** ${bridge.sourceConcept || '?'} (${bridge.sourceAuthor}) ↔ ` +
  `${bridge.targetConcept || '?'} (${bridge.targetAuthor})\n` +
  `${bridge.bridge || ''}\n\n` +
  `Both authors (${bridge.sourceAuthor} and ${bridge.targetAuthor}) MUST be cited `
Hook record verbatim: {"id":"hook-de-anima-07","sourceText":"Aristotle - De Anima","sourceConcept":"Summary Matrix","targetText":"","targetConcept":"","title":"Summary Matrix","bridge":"","relevance":"","tag":"INTERP-high"}
cross-author-utils.ts:365  `if (!text) return 'Unknown';`  // deriveAuthor('') -> 'Unknown'
findings.failure_scenario: Simulated the exact sort+slice for topics ['boredom','attunement','pedagogy'], ['phantasia','imagination','aristotle'] and ['zzzzz','qqqqqq'] — all three return hook-de-anima-07. The rendered prompt section reads: '**Bridge [hook-de-anima-07]:** Summary Matrix (Aristotle) ↔ ? (Unknown)' followed by 'Both authors (Aristotle and Unknown) MUST be cited with direct textual evidence when integrating this bridge.'
findings.consequence: A mandatory, high-confidence-framed instruction to fabricate a cross-author synthesis with a non-existent author, injected into the drafting prompt for a doctoral dissertation. 'Summary Matrix' is a markdown heading the compiler mistook for a concept. This is the single most fabrication-inducing line in the read path.
findings.fix_sketch: Reject empty-concept hooks at load; add `|| 'Unknown'`-style guards at the template AND refuse to emit the section when either author is Unknown. ~15 lines across two files. Also delete or repair the ~10 heading-derived pseudo-hooks ('Connection', 'Specific hooks', 'Integration points', 'Summary Table') upstream.

findings.claim: `_hooksDerivationDone` is a module-global one-shot with NO reset anywhere in the repository, while the object it guards is replaced by a fresh parse on every mtime change.
findings.evidence:
:56   `let _hooksDerivationDone = false;`
:342  `  if (!_hooksDerivationDone) {`
:345  `        hook.sourceAuthor = deriveAuthor(hook.sourceText);`
:351  `    _hooksDerivationDone = true;`
jsonl-loaders.ts:210-213 `const raw = readFileSync(indexPath, 'utf-8'); const parsed = JSON.parse(raw); _compiledIndexCache = { data: parsed, ... };`
`grep -rn "_hooksDerivationDone" src/ tests/ scripts/` returns EXACTLY those three lines. Data: 0 of 72 hooks carry a `sourceAuthor` key on disk (verified by key-frequency count), so :345/:348 is the only source.
findings.failure_scenario: A long-running daemon (`npm run observe` / `memory:start` / `ucm:start`, all in package.json) calls getActiveBridges once. Someone runs the compiler. mtime changes. jsonl-loaders.ts:206 detects it and returns a FRESH parse — hooks with no sourceAuthor/targetAuthor. `_hooksDerivationDone` is still true, so :342 skips derivation forever. Every hook now has `sourceAuthor === undefined`.
findings.consequence: Two silent failures at once. (a) icp-orchestrator.ts:366-368 `if (bridge.sourceAuthor && ...) requiredAuthors.add(...)` — undefined is falsy, set stays empty, `if (requiredAuthors.size < 2) continue;` fires and cross-author retrieval backfill dies. (b) gold-standard-prompt-builder.ts:712-715 template-interpolates undefined, so the prompt literally reads 'Summary Matrix (undefined) ↔ ? (undefined)' and 'Both authors (undefined and undefined) MUST be cited'. Neither is logged.
findings.fix_sketch: Delete the flag. Derive lazily per hook (`hook.sourceAuthor ??= deriveAuthor(...)`), or key the flag to the cached object identity (`let _derivedFor: object|null = null; if (_derivedFor !== parsed) {...}`). ~6 lines.

findings.claim: `clearJSONLCaches()` nulls `_compiledIndexCache` but has no knowledge of `_hooksDerivationDone` in the other module, so calling it deterministically triggers the undefined-author bug — it is a loaded gun with a live caller path.
findings.failure_scenario: Any call to `clearEdgeCache()` (exported from quality-integration.ts, currently zero callers — I grepped src/, scripts/, tests/) forces the next `getCompiledIndex()` to re-parse into fresh objects with `_hooksDerivationDone` still true. Every downstream author field is undefined from that point until process exit.
findings.consequence: The intended 'clear caches for testing' escape hatch is the fastest way to permanently corrupt the runtime. It is dead today, which means the corruption is latent and untested — the first person who wires up a cache-clear (e.g. after a recompile) silently breaks cross-author retrieval.
findings.fix_sketch: Either export a `resetDerivation()` from cross-author-utils and call it from clearJSONLCaches, or (better) eliminate the flag entirely so nothing needs coordinating. ~10 lines.

findings.claim: The ONLY reader of compiled-index.json wraps everything in a bare `catch {}` that returns null with no log, no counter, and no distinction between 'file absent', 'permission denied' and 'JSON is corrupt'.
findings.failure_scenario: The compiler is re-running and compiled-index.json is half-written when a drafting session reads it. `JSON.parse` throws. Returns null. cross-author-utils.ts:339 `if (!parsed) return null;` -> getActiveBridges :454 returns [] -> icp-orchestrator.ts:361 `continue`. corpus-index-provider.ts:106 returns `{ontologyLines:[],hookLines:[],tensionLines:[]}`. retrieval-stage.ts:477 only logs when the arrays are NON-empty: `if (ontologyLines.length > 0 || ...) goldLog(...)`. Net effect: total index blackout, zero log lines, a normal-looking draft.
findings.consequence: The entire ontology/hook/tension layer can be offline for an entire session and nothing in the system says so. This is the failure mode with the widest blast radius and the least observability in the whole read path.
findings.fix_sketch: `catch (e) { process.stderr.write(\`[jsonl-loaders] compiled-index load FAILED: ${e}\`); return null; }` plus an `existsSync`-vs-parse-error distinction, plus a non-empty log at retrieval-stage.ts:477. ~8 lines.

findings.claim: `buildCorpusCatalog` defaults every title with a missing authority_tier to 'secondary', mislabelling 71 of 117 works — including Heidegger's *The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics* and the Greek critical editions of De Anima, Physics and Rhetoric — as SECONDARY SCHOLARSHIP in the prompt that defines the corpus for the LLM.
findings.evidence:
:317  `      const tier = manifest.titleAuthority.get(title) || 'secondary';`
:327  `  if (secondary.length > 0) sections.push('SECONDARY SCHOLARSHIP:', ...secondary);`
:154-156 (the only writer): `if (titleRaw && meta.authority_tier) { titleAuthority.set(titleRaw, meta.authority_tier); }`
Manifest data: 787 of 835 status=ok records have NO authority_tier. titleAuthority ends with 46 entries; authorTitles holds 117 titles. 71 fall through to 'secondary'.
Actual mislabelled entries include: `Heidegger, Martin | The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics`, `Aristotle | De Anima (Ross_Greek)`, `Aristotle | Ars Rhetorica (Greek, Rudolf Kassel)`, `Aristotle | Physica (Greek, W. D. Ross)`, `Lanham, Richard A. | Analyzing Prose`, `Salvo, Dalton | MA Submission - Veri(dis)similitude...`.
findings.failure_scenario: llm-decomposition-provider.ts:102-103 calls `buildCorpusCatalog()` and injects the result. The model is told GA 29/30 — the source text of the entire boredom analysis — is secondary scholarship, and that the Greek Kassel Rhetorica is secondary scholarship.
findings.consequence: Directly attacks the primary/secondary distinction the dissertation's citation rigor depends on. The model will hedge or mis-frame citations to primary texts because the corpus catalog told it they are commentary. 61% of the catalog is mislabelled.
findings.fix_sketch: Emit a third bucket 'UNCLASSIFIED' rather than silently defaulting, and log the count. ~6 lines here; the durable fix is backfilling authority_tier in the manifest (787 records).

findings.claim: `authorTitles` is only populated when BOTH author_raw and title_raw exist, so the catalog headed 'only suggest from this list' lists 117 of the 578 titles in the corpus — it declares 80% of the ingested corpus non-existent.
findings.failure_scenario: Every VR-pedagogy, boredom-secondary, RDR2-secondary and Part-III source ingested with a unit-style title_raw ('bor-sec-04', 'DISS-04-G28-tier-a', 'phase2-uex-m5') and no author_raw is absent from the catalog. The model is instructed not to suggest them.
findings.consequence: Two compounding losses. (a) The decomposition prompt actively steers away from 80% of the corpus. (b) `isValidAuthorTitlePair` returns false at :254 (`if (!authorTitleList || authorTitleList.length === 0) return false;`) for every one of those works, so any correct citation of them is flagged invalid. This is the single largest coverage gap in the read path and it is entirely invisible — no count, no warning.
findings.fix_sketch: Log `authorTitles` size vs distinct title_raw count at load. Then either backfill author_raw or add an 'UNATTRIBUTED WORKS' section. ~10 lines here; the real fix is upstream in the manifest schema (title_raw is being used as a unit ID, which is a separate modelling error).

findings.claim: `expandQueryWithOntology` anchors its match with `\b`, which in a non-unicode JS RegExp treats Greek letters as non-word characters — so NO Greek-script ontology node name can EVER match, in any query.
findings.evidence:
:179  `        const re = new RegExp('\\b' + escapeRegex(t) + '\\b', 'i');`
Verified in node v22.22.0: `/\bψυχή\b/i.test('the ψυχή of')` === false; `/\bψυχή\b/i.test('theψυχή')` === false; `/\bphantasia\b/i.test('the phantasia of')` === true.
Data: 112 of 701 ontology node names are Greek script.
findings.failure_scenario: retrieval-stage.ts:175 calls `expandQueryWithOntology(retrievalQueries[i], compiledIdx.ontologyNodes)` on a query containing 'ψυχή'. The ψυχή node never matches, so its transliteration ('psyche') and Greek variant are never added to the query. The same query written as 'psyche' DOES match and expands.
findings.consequence: 16% of the ontology is permanently unreachable through query expansion, and reachability depends on which script the user happened to type. The failure is total and silent — `matched` is simply false.
findings.fix_sketch: Add the `u` flag and use `(?<![\p{L}\p{N}])…(?![\p{L}\p{N}])` lookarounds, or drop the boundary and use a tokenizer. ~5 lines.

findings.claim: getActiveBridges matches Latin-script topic words against Greek-script hook concepts by substring containment, which can never succeed — 50 of 72 hooks have a Greek sourceConcept and are matchable only by accident of their German/English target.
findings.evidence:
:473  `    const matchesSource = normalizedTopics.some(t => sourceLower.includes(t) || t.includes(sourceLower));`
Data: 50 of 72 hooks have Greek characters in sourceConcept (e.g. `"sourceConcept": "φαντασία"`), 12 in targetConcept.
Simulated: topic word 'phantasia' vs sourceConcept 'φαντασία' — `'φαντασία'.includes('phantasia')` false, `'phantasia'.includes('φαντασία')` false. The hook-de-anima-02 match in scripts/verify-hardening.ts succeeds ONLY because its targetConcept is 'Erschlossenheit / Being-in-the-World' and the test query contains the literal German word.
findings.failure_scenario: A facet about 'phantasia and perception in Aristotle' cannot reach any of the 50 Greek-source hooks. It falls through to the empty-targetConcept always-match set and returns hook-de-anima-07.
findings.consequence: The bridge layer is blind to exactly the concepts it was built to bridge. Note the ontology nodes DO carry `transliteration` (170 nodes) and `greek` (448 nodes) — the data to fix this exists and is simply not consulted at this call site.
findings.fix_sketch: Normalize both sides through the ontology's greek/transliteration/aliases before comparing, i.e. resolve concept strings to node IDs at load and match on IDs. ~40 lines, and it requires the hooks to carry concept IDs rather than free-text — a compiler-side change.

findings.claim: The tag-confidence tie-break tests for the substring 'medium', but every medium-confidence hook in the corpus is tagged 'INTERP-med' — so the middle tier scores 0, identical to INTERP-low.
findings.evidence:
:489-490:
  `    const confA = a.tag?.includes('high') ? 2 : a.tag?.includes('medium') ? 1 : 0;
     const confB = b.tag?.includes('high') ? 2 : b.tag?.includes('medium') ? 1 : 0;`
Data: the only tag values present are `INTERP-high` (58), `INTERP-med` (8), `INTERP-low` (6). Verified in node: hooks whose tag `.includes('medium')` === 0.
findings.failure_scenario: Two hooks tie on computeMatchScore, one INTERP-med and one INTERP-low. Both get confidence 0, so the tie falls to `(a.id || '').localeCompare(b.id || '')` at :494 — alphabetical ID order decides which single bridge is injected, in preference to the more confident record.
findings.consequence: The confidence ranking silently collapses from three tiers to two. Combined with the cap of 1, low-confidence hooks can and do win over medium-confidence ones on pure ID ordering.
findings.fix_sketch: `.includes('med')` or, better, a `TAG_RANK: Record<string, number>` lookup that throws/logs on an unrecognized tag. ~4 lines.

findings.claim: `extractTopicWords` — the producer — keeps words of length >= 4, but both consumers immediately discard anything under 5, so every 4-character term is silently dropped between the two calls that always appear together.
findings.evidence:
:608-614 (producer):
  `  return text
       .split(/\s+/)
       .map(w => w.replace(/[^a-zA-ZÀ-ÿα-ωΑ-Ω\-]/g, ''))
       .filter(w => w.length >= 4);`
:460-462 (consumer): `  const normalizedTopics = facetTopicWords
     .filter(w => w.length >= 5)
     .map(w => w.toLowerCase());`
:516-518: identical filter in getActiveTensions.
Call sites always pair them: icp-orchestrator.ts:359-360, gold-standard-prompt-builder.ts:702-703 and :1067-1068, write-pipeline-orchestrator.ts:858-859.
findings.failure_scenario: Simulated a facet named 'The soul, the body, and the mind'. extractTopicWords yields ['soul','body','mind']; getActiveBridges filters all three out; `if (normalizedTopics.length === 0) return [];` at :464 returns empty. The most central terms in the entire corpus produce zero bridges and zero tensions.
findings.consequence: 'soul', 'nous', 'body', 'time', 'form', 'eidos' (5, borderline), 'doxa', 'hexis' — the load-bearing four-letter vocabulary of an Aristotle/Heidegger dissertation is structurally excluded. And the exclusion looks identical to 'no bridge is relevant'.
findings.fix_sketch: Make the threshold one constant shared by producer and consumers, and exempt any word that appears in `canonicalTerms`/ontology names regardless of length (that protected-term set already exists at smart-retrieval-layer.ts:794). ~15 lines.

findings.claim: `expandQueryWithCanonicalTerms` matches node names by bare substring with no word boundary, so ordinary English words that merely CONTAIN a node name trigger Greek-term injection into the embedding query.
findings.evidence:
:577-578:
  `    const hasName = name.length >= 4 && queryLower.includes(name);
     const hasTranslit = translit.length >= 4 && queryLower.includes(translit);`
Data: 74 node names are 4-6 characters, including 'form', 'soul', 'time', 'image', 'place', 'cause', 'truth', 'sound', 'style', 'matter', 'nature', 'memory', 'desire', 'logos'.
findings.failure_scenario: Ran the real logic on 'How does Aristotle describe the transformation of information in the soul?' — the substrings inside 'transformation' and 'information' fire the 'Form' node. Output: 'How does Aristotle describe the transformation of information in the soul? (εἶδος, eidos, form / species, ψυχή, psyche)'. The query sent to gte-Qwen2 at smart-retrieval-layer.ts:888 now carries εἶδος because the word 'information' was present.
findings.consequence: Systematic semantic pollution of every retrieval query. The injected terms shift the embedding toward Aristotelian hylomorphism on queries that have nothing to do with it. There is no cap on how many terms get appended and no log of which node fired.
findings.fix_sketch: Word-boundary match with the `u` flag (see the sibling implementation at corpus-index-provider.ts:179, which has the opposite bug), plus a cap on appended terms and a debug log of the firing node names. ~12 lines.

findings.claim: Fixed absolute caps (12 nodes / 3 hooks / 5 tensions) discard the large majority of scoring candidates with no count, no log, and no proportionality to corpus size.
findings.failure_scenario: retrieval-stage.ts:470-473 passes exactly those defaults. 55 relevant ontology nodes are dropped on the floor. The log at :477 reports '12 nodes, 0 hooks, 5 tensions' — it reports what survived, never what was cut.
findings.consequence: The caps are ABSOLUTE, not proportional. At 100x corpus volume the emitted context is byte-identical in size while the discard rate rises from ~82% to ~99.8%. This is the architectural ceiling, and it is already binding at 1x.
findings.fix_sketch: Budget by token count, not record count, and log `emitted/scored`. ~20 lines. The deeper fix is a scoring function worth ranking on (see the scoreCandidate finding) — a fixed cap over a bad ranking is worse than no cap.

findings.claim: Definitions are hard-truncated to 200 characters mid-word, discarding 37.2% of all definition text in the index.
findings.evidence:
:124  `    const defPart = node.definition ? `: ${node.definition.slice(0, 200)}` : '';`
Data: 462 of 701 nodes have definitions longer than 200 chars. Total definition text 196,278 chars; at most 123,267 can ever be rendered; 73,011 chars (37.2%) are unreachable.
Actual rendered line: `- **Boredom proneness**: Stable individual susceptibility to boredom, operationalized chiefly by the Boredom Proneness Scale (Farmer & Sundberg 1986) and the Zuckerman Boredom Susceptibility Scale. Elpidorou & Freeman argue p [bor-sec-04, ...]` — cut mid-word at 'argue p'.
findings.failure_scenario: Any node with a definition over 200 chars (66% of them) reaches the prompt as a fragment ending mid-sentence, with no ellipsis and no indication that it was cut.
findings.consequence: For a project whose stated goal is 'every claim and every clause', the richest field in each record is beheaded at a byte count. Worse, the truncation is invisible to the model, which may treat the fragment as the complete definition.
findings.fix_sketch: Truncate on a sentence boundary and append '…', or budget the whole context block in tokens rather than per-field character slices. ~10 lines.

findings.claim: Of the ten fields every ontology node carries, only four ever reach a prompt: translation, type, text, aliases and centralityTier are never rendered by any code path.
findings.evidence:
:113-116 (searchText — what is SCORED): `[node.name, node.greek, node.transliteration, node.definition, ...(node.aliases || [])]`
:120-127 (what is RENDERED): greek-or-name, transliteration, definition[0:200], units[0:5].
Data: all 701 nodes carry all 10 keys (name, greek, transliteration, translation, definition, type, units, text, aliases, centralityTier).
Measured end-to-end: for topic 'The phenomenology of boredom in VR pedagogy and attunement' the full emitted block is 5,271 chars against a 656,755-char index — 0.803%.
findings.failure_scenario: Node 'Soul' carries `"text": "Aristotle - Complete Works"` (its provenance) and `"type": "core"` (its role). Neither is rendered, so the prompt cannot tell the model which work a concept comes from or how central it is. `aliases` is scored but never shown, so the model never learns the alternate names it is being matched on.
findings.consequence: This is the concrete measurement behind 'carries ontology CONCEPT NAMES and little else': 0.8% of the compiled index reaches the model on a well-matched topic, and provenance is entirely absent. Nothing in this pipeline can support claim-level or clause-level work as written.
findings.fix_sketch: Not a patch — the renderer needs a record schema with provenance (source doc, locator, offsets) and a budgeted serializer. ~150 lines of new code plus a compiler-side schema change.

findings.claim: `dependencyRelation` and `conflictRelation` — the two fields that carry the actual analytic content of a tension — are neither searched nor rendered by any consumer.
findings.evidence:
cross-author-utils.ts:525  `    const searchText = [te.nodeA, te.nodeB, te.description].filter(Boolean).join(' ').toLowerCase();`
corpus-index-provider.ts:148  `    const searchText = [te.nodeA, te.nodeB, te.description].filter(Boolean).join(' ');`
corpus-index-provider.ts:156  `    return `- TENSION [${id}]: ${te.nodeA} ↔ ${te.nodeB} — ${descSnippet}${unitsPart}`;`
Both fields are declared in the interfaces (cross-author-utils.ts:41-42, corpus-index-provider.ts:45-46) and present on all 64 tension records.
Example discarded content (CT-01): `"conflictRelation": "Metaphysical sen…"`, `"dependencyRelation": "Rhetorical energeia presupposes metaphysical sense (activity/aliveness as mode of being)"`.
findings.failure_scenario: A facet whose topic words appear only in `conflictRelation` (e.g. a section specifically about the conflict) never activates that tension — `searchText` does not contain them. And when a tension IS activated, the prompt receives the two node labels and a truncated description but not the stated dependency or conflict.
findings.consequence: The tension layer, whose entire purpose is to surface disagreement, ships without the disagreement. quality-integration.ts:855 then gates generated text on 'tension awareness' using records the model was never shown properly.
findings.fix_sketch: Add both fields to searchText and to the rendered line. ~6 lines — this is the cheapest high-value fix in the whole read path.

findings.claim: getActiveBridges activates on `sourceConcept`/`targetConcept` only; the `bridge` prose (the actual interpretive argument), `title`, and `relevance` are never consulted for matching — and `relevance` is never read anywhere in the repository.
findings.evidence:
:469-470:
  `    const sourceLower = (hook.sourceConcept || '').toLowerCase();
     const targetLower = (hook.targetConcept || '').toLowerCase();`
:473-474 use only those two.
Data: all 72 hooks carry `bridge` and `relevance` keys. `relevance` appears in the interface at :28 (`relevance?: string;`) and in corpus-index-provider.ts:37, and is read by neither module nor by any consumer I grepped.
findings.failure_scenario: hook-de-anima-03's bridge text is 'The critical parallel lies in the *receptive* character of both *aisthēsis* and *Befindlichkeit*.' A facet about 'receptivity' matches nothing — 'receptive' appears only in the bridge prose, which is not searched. Meanwhile corpus-index-provider.ts:132 DOES search `hook.bridge`, so the two consumers of the same data disagree about what a hook match means.
findings.consequence: The most informative field on each hook is inert for activation in the module that gates the mandatory bridge injection, and dead everywhere for `relevance`. Two divergent matching semantics over one dataset also means the hooks shown as 'context' (corpus-index-provider) and the hook injected as 'mandatory' (cross-author-utils) are selected by different rules and routinely disagree.
findings.fix_sketch: Single shared match function over a single field list. ~25 lines to unify, and it forces a decision about what a hook match means.

findings.claim: Selection at the cap boundary is decided by JSON array order, not relevance — 37 candidates tie at the cutoff score for a typical topic and there is no secondary tie-break.
findings.evidence:
:118  `  }).filter(s => s.score > 0).sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score).slice(0, maxNodes);`
:135 and :150 have the same single-key comparator.
Measured: topic 'Aristotle on phantasia and desire' — cutoff score is 1, and 37 of the 44 scoring nodes are tied at 1 for 12 slots. Topic 'on the soul' — cutoff 1, 18 tied. Topic 'nous and time' — cutoff 2, 14 tied.
findings.failure_scenario: V8's sort is stable, so which 12 of 44 nodes reach the prompt is fixed by their index in compiled-index.json. The compiler's `deduplicate_ontology_nodes` and dict iteration change that order between builds. Two recompiles of an unchanged corpus can therefore yield a different 12-node context for the same topic, with no score difference to justify it.
findings.consequence: Prompt context is not reproducible across index builds even when the underlying corpus is unchanged. Combined with the unconditional `builtAt` stamp (compiled-index.json carries `"builtAt": "2026-07-20T16:03:58.499584+00:00"`), there is no way to reproduce a drafting session's inputs.
findings.fix_sketch: Add a deterministic secondary key (`|| a.node.name.localeCompare(b.node.name)`) and a tertiary on a stable node ID. ~3 lines — but it only makes an arbitrary choice reproducible, it does not make it correct.

findings.claim: `scoreCandidate` counts raw substring occurrences with a global regex, no word boundary and no length normalization, so long definitions outrank short exact matches and unrelated records score on incidental substrings.
findings.failure_scenario: A 900-char definition mentioning 'time' three times outscores the canonical 'Time' node's 200-char definition mentioning it twice. The cap then keeps the noisy record and drops the canonical one.
findings.consequence: Ranking is dominated by definition length. On a 100x corpus the number of records with incidental substring hits grows linearly while the 12 slots do not, so the canonical nodes get squeezed out entirely.
findings.fix_sketch: Word-boundary matching with the `u` flag, TF normalized by candidate length, and a field-weighted score (name > transliteration > aliases > definition). ~30 lines. Realistically this should be replaced by embedding similarity against the same vector store the corpus already uses.

findings.claim: Both loaders read entire files into a single JS string; `readFileSync(path,'utf-8')` throws ERR_STRING_TOO_LONG above 536,870,888 chars. reasoning.jsonl is 21.5 MB today — the hard wall is ~25x, not 100x — and the two loaders fail differently.
findings.evidence:
:89   `  const raw = readFileSync(edgePath, 'utf-8');`   // NOT inside try/catch
:90   `  const lines = raw.split('\n').filter(l => l.trim());`
:210  `    const raw = readFileSync(indexPath, 'utf-8');`  // INSIDE the try at :202
Measured: `require('buffer').constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH` === 536870888 on node v22.22.0. god-reason/reasoning.jsonl is 21,498,945 bytes -> 536870888/21498945 = 24.97x. Timed: read+split+parse of the current file takes 150 ms on the main thread.
findings.failure_scenario: Corpus grows 25x. `loadReasoningEdgesSync` at :89 throws an UNCAUGHT RangeError and the process dies. `loadCompiledIndex` at :210 would hit the same wall but the bare catch at :215 swallows it and returns null — total silent index blackout instead of a crash.
findings.consequence: Two different failure modes for the same root cause, neither of which produces a diagnosable message. Additionally `raw.split('\n')` at :53/:90/:130/:166 doubles peak memory and blocks the event loop for 150 ms today — 3.75 s at 25x, on every cache miss, synchronously, inside daemons.
findings.fix_sketch: Stream with `readline`/`createInterface` over a file handle, or use `node:fs` line iteration; keep an explicit dropped/parsed counter. ~40 lines per loader. This is unavoidable before any volume increase.

findings.claim: The `CrossPipelineHook` interface declares `sourceAuthor: string` and `targetAuthor: string` as REQUIRED, and the loader casts untyped JSON straight to it — so TypeScript actively certifies as non-nullable the exact two fields that are undefined on disk and become undefined again after the derivation bug.
findings.evidence:
:30-33:
  `  /** Derived at load time from sourceText (e.g., "Aristotle" from "Aristotle - De Anima") */
     sourceAuthor: string;
     /** Derived at load time from targetText */
     targetAuthor: string;`
:338  `  const parsed = loadCompiledIndexShared(projectRoot) as CompiledIndex | null;`
jsonl-loaders.ts:198  `export function loadCompiledIndex(projectRoot?: string): any | null {`
Data: 0 of 72 hooks carry a sourceAuthor key on disk.

findings.claim: deriveAuthor's final fallback returns the first manifest author whose key (>= 5 chars) appears anywhere as a substring of the input, in Map insertion order — producing confident misattributions.

findings.consequence: Fabricated attribution with no confidence signal and no log. Compounded by the fact that Map iteration order is manifest file order, so which author wins depends on ingestion sequence rather than on match quality.

findings.claim: All three mtime caches key on floating-point millisecond mtime alone, with no size or content check, so a sub-millisecond rewrite is invisible.

findings.failure_scenario: Two writes within the same millisecond (scripted recompile, `cp` preserving timestamps, a container layer restore, or a symlink retarget onto a file whose inode mtime is unchanged) leave the cache serving stale content for the life of the process.
findings.consequence: Low probability per event, but the consequence is indistinguishable from correct operation and there is no way to detect it from the outside. Noted in tmp/SYSTEM-ANALYSIS-2026-04-30/SYSTEM-ANALYSIS-REPORT.md:154 as unverified; it remains unverified and unfixed.

findings.claim: `buildCorpusCatalog` concatenates one line per (author, title) with no cap and is injected verbatim into every decomposition prompt — it grows linearly with the corpus and has no token budget.

prior_claim_verdicts.prior_claim: _hooksDerivationDone (cross-author-utils.ts:56, guard :342, set :351) is a one-shot global with NO reset anywhere; jsonl-loaders.ts:205-213 invalidates on mtime and returns a FRESH graph; 0 of 72 hooks carry sourceAuthor, so derivation at :344-349 is the only source. Recompile mid-process empties requiredAuthors, then icp-orchestrator.ts:368 hits a continue, and cross-author backfill silently dies with no log line
prior_claim_verdicts.evidence: Line numbers exact: :56 `let _hooksDerivationDone = false;`, :342 `if (!_hooksDerivationDone) {`, :351 `_hooksDerivationDone = true;`. `grep -rn "_hooksDerivationDone"` over src/, tests/, scripts/ returns EXACTLY those three lines — no reset exists. jsonl-loaders.ts:205-213 confirmed: stat, compare, `readFileSync`+`JSON.parse` producing fresh objects. Key-frequency count over compiled-index.json: `{'id':72,'sourceText':72,'sourceConcept':72,'targetText':72,'targetConcept':72,'title':72,'bridge':72,'relevance':72,'tag':72}` — sourceAuthor appears 0 times. icp-orchestrator.ts:368 `if (requiredAuthors.size < 2) continue;` confirmed verbatim.
prior_claim_verdicts.correction: Two corrections, both making it worse. (1) 'no log line' is not quite right — icp-orchestrator.ts:364 DOES log `[ICP-Stage6b] Bridge activated: ...` immediately before the continue. What is unlogged is the SKIP itself, which is worse than silence: the log affirms the bridge activated, then the backfill is abandoned with no further output, so the trace reads as success. (2) The claim understates the trigger. Recompile is not the only path — `clearJSONLCaches()` (jsonl-loaders.ts:305-310, reachable via quality-integration.ts:411 `clearEdgeCache`) nulls `_compiledIndexCache` without touching the flag, and any caller passing a non-cwd `projectRoot` thrashes the single-entry path-keyed cache (jsonl-loaders.ts:206) so the fresh parse happens on the SECOND call. Additionally the downstream effect is not only the ICP continue: gold-standard-prompt-builder.ts:712-715 and :1077-1080 interpolate the fields with no fallback, so the prompt renders 'Summary Matrix (undefined) ↔ ? (undefined)' and 'Both authors (undefined and undefined) MUST be cited'.
